false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

The handler explicitly authorizes non-organizers (team admins/owners and attendees), but then loads credentials with getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and constructs EventManager from the caller. The calendar event and destination calendar belong to booking.user/organizer, so for those authorized non-organizer callers EventManager cannot use the organizer's calendar credential and the external calendar attendee update can silently fail while the database and emails succeed, leaving systems inconsistent. The booking organizer's credentials/user should be used.

Dialog state is not reset when closed without Cancel

multiEmailValue and isInvalidEmail are only cleared by the explicit Cancel button or on mutation success. Closing the dialog through the dialog close affordance, Escape, or overlay only calls setIsOpenDialog, so previously typed emails and a stale validation error remain the next time the dialog is opened and can be submitted accidentally. Editing the emails also does not clear isInvalidEmail after the user fixes the input.

Guest list has no maximum length

The input schema accepts an arbitrarily large guests array. The handler then creates all attendees, loads a translation per attendee, updates the calendar, and sends email to the organizer/team plus every attendee. Any authorized caller, including an attendee, can use this for large-scale email fan-out/resource consumption and send platform-generated meeting invitations to many arbitrary addresses; the server should enforce a reasonable cap.

Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, pending, or past bookings

The handler never checks booking.status or booking.endTime before creating attendees, updating the calendar, and sending guests-added/scheduled emails with a CONFIRMED ICS. A direct API caller can therefore mutate a cancelled, rejected, unconfirmed, or already-ended booking and cause new calendar/email invitations to be sent for an event that is not an accepted upcoming booking.

MultiEmail imports the @calcom/ui barrel from inside the same package

MultiEmail lives in @calcom/ui but imports Button, EmailField, Icon, and Tooltip from the '@calcom/ui' barrel, while that barrel exports MultiEmailLazy which dynamically imports this file. This creates a self-referential import cycle and pulls the whole UI barrel into a component that was specifically made lazy, risking circular-chunk/undefined-import problems and defeating the intended code splitting. The component should import from relative component paths.

No tests cover the new addGuests mutation

This PR adds a new mutation with organizer/team-admin/team-owner/attendee authorization branches, duplicate and blacklist filtering, database writes, calendar updates, and email fan-out, but adds no handler or integration tests. Tests should cover at least outsider rejection, admin versus owner access, organizer/attendee access, duplicate/blacklisted guests, and non-accepted bookings so authorization and filtering regressions are caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increment uses a stale read instead of an atomic increment

Both increments (here and in the catch block at line 195) write `reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value fetched at the start of the run. The handler has no lock and makes slow sequential Twilio calls, so overlapping cron invocations can both read retryCount 0, both fail, and both write 1, losing increments and potentially keeping a permanently failing reminder below the >1 deletion threshold forever. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count deletion is not scoped to unscheduled SMS reminders

The second branch of the deleteMany OR only checks retryCount > 1, without method: SMS or scheduled: false. As written it can delete EMAIL/WHATSAPP WorkflowReminder rows that have retryCount > 1, and can delete an already-scheduled reminder, losing its referenceId so a Twilio message already scheduled can no longer be tracked or cancelled. The retry cleanup should be scoped to SMS (and unscheduled) reminders like the fetch below.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing recipient or message never increments retryCount

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)` when Twilio returns a falsy result, or in the catch block when an exception is thrown. If sendTo is missing/empty (e.g. no smsReminderNumber) or the generated message is empty, the block is skipped entirely: no scheduling attempt, no retryCount increment, and the row stays scheduled:false and is re-fetched on every cron run until its scheduledDate passes. That leaves one of the failure modes this PR is meant to bound retrying indefinitely; the empty-recipient/message case needs an increment or removal path too.

Unhandled update in catch block can abort the whole cron run

The catch block now awaits prisma.workflowReminder.update without any nested error handling. If that update fails — for example the reminder was deleted between findMany and the catch (Prisma P2025), or the original error was a database failure — the exception escapes the per-reminder loop, all remaining unscheduled reminders are never processed, and the handler returns an error instead of continuing. Previously the catch only logged and moved on. The increment should be wrapped so a failure to record the retry is logged without poisoning the rest of the batch.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests were deleted while caching logic remains

This PR removes the entire Caching describe block that verified repeated getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions calls reuse cached results, but InsightsBookingService still maintains cachedAuthConditions and cachedFilterConditions state. No replacement test covers the cached paths, including the cached null filter case, so a regression in cache initialization or invalidation would go undetected. Restore the caching tests adapted to compare Prisma.Sql results instead of Prisma where-objects.

OR authorization/filter fragments are returned without outer parentheses

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition and buildTeamAuthorizationCondition return fragments such as (A AND B) OR (C AND D) with no enclosing parentheses, buildFilterConditions similarly returns an unparenthesized eventType OR at line 106, and getBaseConditions returns these fragments unwrapped when only one kind of condition exists. Because AND binds tighter than OR in SQL, a caller composing the public result as WHERE ${conditions} AND <date or status condition> will apply the extra condition only to the last OR branch; the first team-booking branch will ignore it, returning rows outside the requested range/filter. Wrap each top-level returned condition in parentheses so the fragments are safely composable.

Public findMany method removed without migrating callers

The conversion deletes InsightsBookingService.findMany, which previously queried BookingTimeStatusDenormalized with the authorization and filter conditions, and replaces it with getBaseConditions returning only a Prisma.Sql fragment. No caller is updated in this PR, so any existing consumer calling service.findMany(...) will fail TypeScript compilation and lose the previous query behavior (including merging caller-supplied where/select arguments). Migrate all call sites to $queryRaw with getBaseConditions in the same change, or keep a compatible findMany wrapper.

Team/org ANY(array) SQL is never executed against the database

The team-scope (line 278) and org-scope (line 305) tests only assert equality between two locally constructed Prisma.sql objects. The sole executed $queryRaw test at line 481 uses user scope, which contains no array parameter. Therefore the new "teamId" = ANY(${number[]}) and "userId" = ANY(${number[]}) parameter binding is never verified against PostgreSQL; if Prisma/Postgres cannot infer or encode the JS array parameter for these queries, both scopes fail at runtime while all tests pass. Add executed $queryRaw integration tests for team and org scopes asserting the returned booking ids.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Committed tunnelmole helper is macOS-only, cwd-dependent, and masks failures

`sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS syntax and fails under GNU sed on Linux; ENV_FILE='../.env' resolves relative to the caller's working directory rather than the script/repo root, so running it from the repo root writes ../.env outside the repo; and cleanup() always exits 0, so the failure paths at the tunnel-URL check report success to callers. This unrelated dev script should be fixed or removed from the feature PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ownership failure is thrown as a generic 500 error

When the credential does not exist or does not belong to the caller, the handler throws a plain Error('Credential not found or access denied'). tRPC will surface this as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR rather than a client error such as TRPCError with NOT_FOUND/FORBIDDEN, polluting server-error monitoring and giving API consumers the wrong contract for an expected authorization outcome.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is always formatted with the en-US locale

The cache_last_updated timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', ...)` regardless of the user's locale from useLocale. Non-English users will see US date/time formatting in an otherwise localized UI; format with the active locale instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache deletion ignores disableConnectionModification gating

canDisconnect respects delegationCredentialId and disableConnectionModification, but hasCache is computed only from integration type and cacheUpdatedAt, and the early return is `if (!canDisconnect && !hasCache)`. On screens that set disableConnectionModification to make the connection read-only/managed, a Google credential with cache still renders the dropdown and enables the destructive delete-cache mutation, defeating the flag that hides disconnect in the same UI.

Deleting cache does not refresh the connected-calendars query

deleteCacheMutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike disconnectMutation below it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. In SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper onChanged is optional and often undefined, so after a successful deletion the dropdown keeps showing the old cacheUpdatedAt timestamp and 'Delete cached data' action until a manual refetch, contradicting the success toast.

Every cache refresh rewrites all SelectedCalendar rows via an empty update

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(credential.id, {}) on every cache population. That performs a write touching updatedAt for every SelectedCalendar row of the credential (including event-type-scoped rows), so updatedAt no longer reflects user selection changes, adds a DB write to a hot availability path, and is not even used by the new UI, which displays CalendarCache.updatedAt via cacheUpdatedAt.

Expired cache entries are reported as active cache

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups all CalendarCache rows for the credentials without filtering on expiresAt. getCachedAvailability treats rows with expiresAt in the past as cache misses, but this method will still return their updatedAt, so the UI displays an expired, unusable cache as present and offers to delete it. Filter to unexpired rows (expiresAt >= now) when computing status.

Handler bypasses the calendar-cache disabled/mock repository selection

The handler directly instantiates the concrete CalendarCacheRepository instead of going through the CalendarCache factory used elsewhere (CalendarCache.init), which returns CalendarCacheRepositoryMock returning [] when calendar-cache is disabled. When the feature is disabled, this endpoint will still query CalendarCache and surface cache status/deletion for leftover rows that the rest of the system intentionally ignores.

No tests for the new cache-status query or ownership-checked deletion

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that deletes data based on credential ownership, a groupBy status query, and a mock implementation, but adds no tests. There is no coverage that another user's credentialId is rejected, that only the caller's credential cache is deleted, or that getCacheStatusByCredentialIds returns the latest updatedAt per credential, so an authorization or mapping regression would ship undetected.

dev:cron now depends on unpinned, undeclared tsx via npx

The script changes `ts-node cron-tester.ts` (ts-node is a declared devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but tsx is not declared anywhere in the workspace dependencies. Running the script will download an unpinned package at runtime, failing offline and introducing version/supply-chain drift; it is also unrelated to the calendar-cache feature. Add tsx as a devDependency or keep ts-node.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Workflow reminder cancellations are fired without being awaited

updatedBookings.forEach(... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...) / deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)) discards the promises returned by these async functions. The handler then awaits only unrelated attendee/reference deletions and returns a 200 response, so there is no guarantee the prisma update setting cancelled=true (or the SMS/Twilio cancellation and row deletion) has completed before the request finishes; in a serverless invocation the work can be cut short after the response, leaving cancelled=false in the database and allowing the cron/SendGrid schedule to send the reminder for the cancelled booking. The surrounding code cannot observe or retry the failure because the promise is dropped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Deferred-only cancellation misses reminders that are due imminently

For a scheduled email this function now only sets cancelled=true and never cancels with SendGrid immediately, regardless of how soon the reminder is due. Cancellation therefore depends entirely on the periodic scheduleEmailReminders cron running before the SendGrid sendAt time. If a booking is cancelled a few minutes before its reminder and the next cron run happens after that time, SendGrid will already have sent the email; the cron's initial deleteMany for past scheduledDate rows then just removes the DB record. The previous immediate-cancellation behaviour covered this last-minute case.

One failing SendGrid cancellation blocks all other cancellations

All reminders are cancelled sequentially inside a single try block, while the Prisma delete operations are only executed by the Promise.all after the loop. If client.request throws for one reminder (for example an invalid, expired, or already-cancelled batch), the catch is taken, none of the queued deletes run, and every later reminder in remindersToCancel is never even attempted. The same failing reminder will be retried first on the next cron run, so other reminders whose scheduled time falls within the next hour can still be dispatched by SendGrid.

Reschedule path bypasses the deferred cancellation mechanism and loses failures

Rescheduling calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true), which immediately POSTs a SendGrid cancellation instead of setting cancelled=true. This reintroduces the exact SendGrid pending-cancellations cap (100) that this PR is meant to work around for rescheduled bookings. Worse, if that POST fails, deleteScheduledEmailReminder only logs the error and returns without deleting the row or setting cancelled, so the scheduleEmailReminders cron (which only looks for cancelled=true) will never retry and the reminder for the old booking time will still be sent.

Workflow deletion uses immediate cancellation then destroys the retry record

Deleting a workflow calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true), which immediately cancels in SendGrid but neither deletes nor marks the WorkflowReminder row; the code then deletes the workflow at line 220, and the WorkflowStep/WorkflowReminder cascade deletes the reminder rows. If the immediate SendGrid cancellation fails (including via the pending-cancellation cap described in the PR, or a transient error), the error is swallowed inside deleteScheduledEmailReminder and the DB record that the new cron-based deferred cancellation could have retried is gone, so the scheduled email will still be sent for a deleted workflow. The same pattern is used when a workflow step is deleted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach leaves calendar/video deletion fire-and-forget

The forEach callback was made async to await getCalendar, but Array.prototype.forEach ignores the returned promises. Reschedule therefore proceeds to send the reschedule email and return true without waiting for calendar.deleteEvent or deleteMeeting to even start (the await on getCalendar defers them past the forEach), so in a request-scoped/serverless execution the old events can be left behind, and any rejection becomes an unhandled rejection that the surrounding try/catch cannot catch. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` or a for...of loop.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are started eagerly for every app

Every value in the appStore object literal is an import() call, so all 28 calls are evaluated as soon as this module is loaded. Code that needs only one app (for example getCalendar for a single credential) therefore still starts loading every calendar, video, CRM, and payment app and retains all of their side effects and memory/startup cost, defeating the intended per-app lazy loading. A rejected import for an app that is never used can also surface later as an unhandled rejection from the cached promise. Store thunks such as `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and invoke the thunk at lookup time instead.

Recurring-cancellation deletions can miss the later Promise.all entirely

For recurring bookings, calendar deletions are collected by pushing into apiDeletes from inside an async forEach callback that first awaits getCalendar and then awaits deleteEvent before pushing. The handler later awaits Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)), but concat snapshots apiDeletes at that moment, typically before those async callbacks have pushed anything. The handler can therefore delete the booking's attendees/references (losing the external uids needed to retry) and return while the external calendar deletions are not awaited or have not run, orphaning events on users' calendars. Collect the deletion promises synchronously via map/Promise.all or a sequential for...of and await them before the database cleanup completes.

requestReschedule does not wait for old calendar/video deletion

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach now takes an async callback whose promise is discarded. Immediately afterwards the mutation sends the reschedule email and webhooks and returns, while the awaited getCalendar/deleteEvent and deleteMeeting work is still pending; it may be abandoned when the request ends and its failures are unhandled, leaving the supposedly cancelled calendar event and video meeting active. Await the deletions with Promise.all over map (or a for...of loop) before continuing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects split schedules and allows days off

The new check returns unavailable when Array.find locates ANY same-weekday working-hour range that the slot start is outside. A host with split hours on one day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) will have a valid 10:00 slot rejected because it is outside the second range. Conversely, if the host has no working-hour entry for that weekday, find returns undefined, execution falls through to the busy check, and the host can be considered available on a day off. Additionally lines 141-142 set both start and end from the slot start, so a slot starting inside working hours but ending after them is never rejected. The predicate must instead require that at least one range fully contains [slotStart, slotEnd].

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty date-override comparison is always false

Line 114 compares two distinct Dayjs objects with ===, which compares object identity and is always false, so the special case for a zero-length override (start equal to end, used to mark a date unavailable) is dead code. A slot straddling that instant (slotStart before it and slotEnd after it) then falls through, dateOverrideExist is true, and the function returns the host as available on a day they marked unavailable. The instants must be compared with isSame/valueOf.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override matching mishandles multiple ranges and boundary-straddling slots

The find callback returns true as soon as the slot is outside the first override for that date, so a slot contained in a second override range on the same date is rejected. The containment test is also incomplete: a slot that starts before an override starts but ends inside it triggers neither the slotEnd<=overrideStart nor slotStart>overrideEnd branch, so it is treated as inside although part of the event lies outside the override; a slot starting exactly at override end is likewise treated as inside because isAfter is false. Slots should be accepted only when some override satisfies slotStart >= overrideStart and slotEnd <= overrideEnd.

No test exercises the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The only added test is a second timezone query on the pre-existing single-user scenario (hosts: [], no ROUND_ROBIN schedulingType). The PR's primary claim - that a fixed host's date override restricts a round-robin event while round-robin hosts remain bookable - and the new checkIfIsAvailable path for fixed/loose hosts are therefore never exercised, so regressions such as split working hours, multiple override ranges, or overrides combined with busy bookings would pass this suite.

Slots inside a date override bypass busy-time checks

When a slot is deemed inside a date override, checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 133-135 before reaching the busy.every check at the end of the function. Therefore a fixed or round-robin host who has a date override covering a time but also has a Cal booking or connected-calendar event at that time is reported available, and the slot remains bookable (for round-robin the host also remains in slot.userIds). Date-override availability must still be intersected with busy times.

Timezone-converted override loses day rollover across midnight

The converted override start/end are reduced to hour()*60+minute(), discarding any day shift produced by adding the invitee-organizer offset. If applying the invitee offset pushes the override end past local midnight, endTime wraps to a small value while startTime stays large, so buildSlots discards the range as start>=end and the override disappears entirely (both the pre-midnight part on the start day and the post-midnight part on the next day, which activeOverrides will not select because the override did not start that day). Minutes outside the 0-1439 range, or an explicit split at midnight, are needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender check raises KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata

The check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. Integrations created through the normal pipeline only get metadata["sender"] when state happens to contain a sender (the updated test's basic flow asserts metadata with no sender key), and integrations created before sender tracking existed likewise lack it. When such an Integration exists but its OrganizationIntegration has been removed, this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of either proceeding or showing the integration-failed page, breaking reinstallation/moving of those integrations. The lookup should use a safe .get() chain and define the behavior when sender is absent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not exist yet

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the Integration.DoesNotExist branch immediately returns pipeline.next_step(), while the github_authenticated_user versus integration.metadata["sender"] comparison at lines 500-505 only runs when an Integration already exists without an OrganizationIntegration. A newly installed GitHub App therefore completes without any sender check if the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration row (a normal race, since GitHub sends the webhook and the user redirect independently) or if the webhook was missed/delayed. An attacker who installed the app can have a different Sentry user claim that installation_id during that window, defeating the validation this PR is intended to add; the check needs to fail closed or obtain the installer identity from a source available at build_integration/finish time rather than relying solely on a pre-existing row.

Token-exchange network errors escape the graceful error handling

OAuthLoginView calls safe_urlopen() before the try block; only safe_urlread()/decoding/parsing is wrapped. If GitHub's access-token endpoint is unreachable, resets the connection, or safe_urlopen rejects/errors on the request, the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 instead of rendering the github-integration-failed page that the PR promises for a failed code exchange. The safe_urlopen call (and the unguarded get_user_info call that follows) should be covered by the same failure path that handles a missing access_token.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The rewritten test supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which does not match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView returns the generic invalid-request page before build_integration/get_installation_info is ever reached. The test therefore passes even if the GitHub 404 handling ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') is broken or removed, and it silently drops the previous coverage/assertion for that message. The test should drive the flow with the correct pipeline state and an installation_id step so the mocked 404 from /app/installations/{id} is what produces the failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time

The dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, so timezone.now() runs once when the class is defined rather than for each AssignmentSource. Every instance created without an explicit queued value therefore shares the process import time, making queued incorrect as a record of when an assignment was queued. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
to_dict produces a non-JSON-serializable Celery argument and breaks round-trip typing

to_dict() uses asdict(), leaving queued as a datetime object. sync_group_assignee_outbound puts this dict directly into sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async kwargs, which must cross Sentry's task serialization boundary; a datetime is not a plain JSON value, and if encoded as an ISO string, from_dict will construct an AssignmentSource whose queued field is a string rather than a datetime. Serialize queued explicitly (for example as an ISO timestamp) and parse it back in from_dict so the round trip is safe and type-consistent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Outbound suppression is only tested for assignment, not deassignment or other integrations

The new matching-source test covers only GroupAssignee.assign. The deassign suppression uses separate branches in GroupAssignee.deassign and in sync_group_assignee_inbound's assign=False path, so a regression there would still echo unassignments back to the originating integration and would not be caught. There is also no test that an assignment sourced from one integration still syncs to a different linked integration, so over-suppression would not be caught either.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with just `pass`, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data. This class implements none of them, so `Detector.detector_handler` calling `group_type.detector_handler(self)` for a metric_alert_fire detector raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class, and process_detectors crashes instead of the previous no-op behaviour where evaluate() returned []. true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The docstring says evaluate "returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult", but this PR changes the signature and implementation to return dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]. Implementers relying on the docstring will implement or consume the wrong return type; update the docstring to describe the dict keyed by group_key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence for the wrong group key

The expected occurrence is built with build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, ...), so its fingerprint is [<detector_id>:val1], but evaluate_group_key_value is then called with group_key "group_key" and value 10, so the handler builds an occurrence with fingerprint [<detector_id>:group_key]. IssueOccurrence equality includes the fingerprint, so the expected DetectorEvaluationResult cannot equal the actual result and this test fails / does not verify the intended dedupe path. Build the expected occurrence with "group_key" (and the value actually passed, 10).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes accepts zero and negative values

The new --flusher-processes option accepts any integer. In SpanFlusher, 0 is treated as unset because it uses `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so `--flusher-processes 0` unexpectedly starts one heavy spawned Sentry/Kafka-producer process per assigned shard. Negative values flow into `min()` and shard modulo indexing, which can raise a KeyError or start no flusher workers during consumer construction. Validate this as a positive integer, for example with click.IntRange(min=1) and equivalent validation in SpanFlusher/ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.

Comma-joined shard list corrupts metrics tags

When one flusher process handles multiple shards, which is the normal case when flusher_processes is smaller than the shard count and always the case for the CLI default of 1, `shard_tag` becomes a value such as `0,1,2`. Passing that comma-containing value as a StatsD/DogStatsD tag makes the backend parse it as `shard:0` plus stray tags `1` and `2`, so the produce, wait-produce, and segment-size metrics cannot be correctly attributed by shard. Emit these metrics per flushed segment/shard or otherwise use a single sanitized shard tag value.

Multi-shard flusher test never flushes any spans

test_flusher_processes_limit creates four shards mapped to two flusher processes, but it only asserts process counts and then joins without submitting spans or advancing the flush clock. The existing basic test covers only one shard/process, so the central new behavior—a shared process correctly flushing, producing, and completing segments for multiple shards, without drops or duplicates—is untested. Add an end-to-end test that stores spans across several shards with fewer flusher processes than shards and asserts the produced segments for each shard.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked offsets make commit checks repeatedly scan an ever-growing set

OffsetTracker retains every offset after a blocked or very slow offset, because offsets can only be removed after a contiguous commit. get_committable_offsets() is called once per second and computes both min() and max() over that retained set each time. During exactly the slow-item backlog this feature is meant to tolerate, the set can grow to a large number of completed offsets and the commit loop becomes repeated O(n) work while also retaining unbounded tracking state.

Close stops offset committing before workers finish and shutdown drops queued work

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() stops and joins the commit thread before shutting down the queue pool, so results completed by workers afterward have no commit loop left to commit their offsets and will be redelivered. In addition, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False); a busy worker exits after its current item instead of draining its queue. Graceful close therefore both leaves processed offsets uncommitted and abandons queued work rather than finishing it within the strategy's join period.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs an exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can consequently commit the offset for a result that was never successfully handled, contradicting the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing and causing failed uptime results to be lost rather than redelivered.

Invalid max_workers values are silently accepted for thread-queue-parallel mode

The CLI accepts any integer for --max-workers, and this code converts 0 to 20 with 'or' while passing a negative value through as num_queues. A negative value creates no queues or workers; submissions then fail with an index/modulo error, are caught by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), and are marked complete, so their offsets can be committed without processing. The option should be validated as a positive integer before constructing the pool.

Python's salted hash does not provide consistent group-to-queue assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() for a string group key. Python randomizes string hashing per interpreter unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed, so the same subscription can map to different queues after a restart or when processed by another consumer process. That undermines the documented consistent-assignment and per-group ordering guarantee across rebalances and deployments; a stable digest such as hashlib.md5 or sha256 should be used instead.

Rebalanced strategy reuses an irreversibly shut-down queue pool

The factory creates FixedQueuePool once during construction, while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts that pool down. Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory when partitions are revoked and reassigned, so the new strategy receives workers that have exited and queues on which shutdown() has already been called. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that exception and marks the offset complete, allowing messages to be committed without being processed. A normal Kafka rebalance can therefore cause silent data loss until the process is restarted.

Unbounded queues provide no Arroyo backpressure

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and therefore has no maximum size, and submit() never raises MessageRejected or otherwise blocks. If workers process more slowly than Kafka delivers, Arroyo can continue submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory use and hiding the backlog from Kafka flow control. This also makes the class documentation's claim of natural backpressure when queues fill up incorrect because these queues never fill.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored

The test named "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}; despite the comment saying this allows access, checkPermission treats a false map value as no permission, and the fake permission store also returns no granting permission. The request therefore denies through the ordinary cached/DB path even if permDenialCache is never consulted, so the test does not prove the new short-circuit works. It should configure the underlying store or permission cache to allow dash1, or assert that the permission store is not called when the denial entry is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous

userPermDenialCacheKey joins variable-length UID, action, name, and parent values with plain underscores and no escaping, length prefixes, or hashing. Distinct tuples can consequently produce the same key: for example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. Grafana resource and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny a different resource until the entry expires. Build the key from a structured, unambiguously encoded or hashed tuple.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include the identity type

The denial key is built only from namespace, the raw subject UID, action, resource name, and parent folder, but permission resolution switches on identity type and returns different permission sets for the same UID. In particular, anonymous and render-service subjects both use UID "0", while anonymous receives Viewer-role permissions and the render service is granted read access to all dashboards and folders. A denial recorded for anonymous:0 can therefore short-circuit and incorrectly deny render:0 for the same dashboard for up to the denial TTL, and the same collision can occur between user and service-account spellings. The key must include the identity type, preferably together with the canonical resolved UID.

Denial entries shadow fresher permissions and undermine immediate access after a grant

Check consults permDenialCache before checking the ordinary permission cache, and neither getUserPermissions' permission-cache refresh nor List's refresh deletes existing denial entries. After a permission is granted, such as the creator permission inserted for a new dashboard or folder, a later check or list for another resource can refresh permCache with a scope map that now allows the denied resource, yet checks for that resource will still return the old denial until the denial TTL expires. A denial recorded by a check made just before the grant has the same effect. This partially defeats the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created resources immediately; cached allowances should be honoured before denials or denials should be invalidated when permissions are refreshed.

Every distinct cached denial now forces a database permission fetch

When cached permissions do not allow a check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the permission-store cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so this performs a fresh database permission query. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent tuple for 30 seconds. A user checking many distinct dashboards or folders they do not own therefore causes one permission query per resource instead of one query per user/action as before, multiplying database load in denial-heavy or enumeration-heavy workloads and increasing cache cardinality. The revalidation needs a freshness or negative-cache strategy that does not scale database queries with the number of distinct denied resources.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key

The switch previously rendered GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}; the replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits the key while the datasource and unknown branches keep theirs. In this dynamically appended/filtered list, index-based reconciliation can reuse the wrong component instance and its local state such as modals, drawers, and menus, in addition to producing React key warnings. Restore key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence action opens no drawer for Prometheus-only rules

In the new list view RuleActionsButtons receives only promRule, so `rule` is undefined. Clicking Silence in AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but this line only mounts SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. The click therefore has no visible effect and silencing from the alert list is broken, even though the new prom abilities may show the Silence menu item.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action is never rendered for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

canDelete can now become true through useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when only a promRule is available, but the Delete menu item is additionally gated by `rulerRule &&` and its handler is typed to require a RulerRuleDTO. In the new GrafanaGroupLoader/FilterView list, rulerRule is always undefined, so users with delete permission cannot delete a rule from the list. The GrafanaGroupLoader test even encodes this by expecting only four menu items despite granting delete permission.

Federated rule groups lose their immutable status

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) for CombinedRules and marked federated rules unsupported for Update/Delete. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which discards the group and hardcodes isFederated to false. Federated Mimir rule groups in existing CombinedRule consumers will therefore be offered edit/delete actions that federated groups do not support.

Grafana recording rules can no longer be paused

The ruler-based ability used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules, for Pause/Restore. The new prom-based ability uses isAlertingRule instead, so Pause and Restore are unsupported for Grafana recording rules. Since the list view no longer supplies a ruler rule to provide the old ability, recording rules lose pause/unpause entirely.

Pause action is never rendered for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

The new list view supplies only a promRule and no rulerRule, and this PR computes canPause from the new Grafana prom abilities. Rendering still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule), which is false when rulerRule is undefined, and MenuItemPauseRule also requires that ruler rule. Consequently Pause never appears in the new rule list even for editable, unpaused Grafana rules, despite the newly added ability check.

skipToken does not actually skip Grafana prom abilities

Callers pass skipToken for cloud rules, non-Grafana prom rules, or absent prom rules, but useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts it to undefined and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities still computes real abilities. For an undefined rule, Duplicate becomes [AlwaysSupported, Grafana-rule-create permission] because provisioned/plugin checks are false and loading is false. AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler result, so Duplicate can appear for cloud or ruler-only rules based solely on an unrelated Grafana create permission. A skipped rule should return [false, false] for every action.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Queries that interpolate to empty are no longer filtered out before sharding

The order was changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate: lines 49-52 test the pre-interpolation expr, so a target such as '$SELECTOR' that resolves to an empty string was previously dropped but now survives into groupTargetsByQueryType, requestSupportsSharding/getSelectorForShardValues and fetchLabelValues with an empty stream selector. It is only dropped later by runSplitQuery's own pre-interpolation filter, which can leave that call with no grouped requests instead of the query simply being ignored as an empty query. Add a post-interpolation expr filter (and apply the same filter-after-interpolate ordering in runSplitQuery).

Shard-split queries are interpolated multiple times

runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target here, but splitQueriesByStreamShard (line 163) then passes those targets to runSplitQuery, which at querySplitting.ts:299 calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables again for every shard/time sub-request; the updated shard test even expects 5 applyTemplateVariables calls for one original query. Loki's applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters adhoc filters into the stream selector and re-runs template replacement, neither of which is guaranteed idempotent: repeated passes can add the same adhoc matcher again and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by a first-pass variable value, besides re-parsing already-interpolated LogQL per chunk. Interpolation should be owned by one layer, e.g. the shard layer should be able to tell runSplitQuery its targets are already interpolated.

Split queries are interpolated again by datasource.runQuery for every chunk

The queries interpolated here are built into grouped sub-requests and executed via datasource.runQuery in runSplitGroupedQueries (line 180). Loki's runQuery backend path (DataSourceWithBackend.query) applies applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and request.filters before sending each chunk to the backend, so every split query is now interpolated at least twice, and three times on the shard path. As with the shard double-interpolation, the repeated adhoc-filter injection from request.filters and repeated templateSrv replacement of already-substituted values are not guaranteed idempotent and can corrupt or invalidly duplicate stream-selector matchers. The early interpolation for splitting decisions needs to be reconciled with the downstream one, rather than simply adding another pass.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil requests panic before LoggerMiddleware's nil guards can run

QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics dereference req.PluginContext without a nil check. LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards nil requests and passes them through (logger_middleware.go:63, 77, 90, 104), but in CreateMiddlewares the contextual middleware sits in front of it (pluginsintegration.go:160-161), so a nil request now panics in this middleware instead of reaching the guarded pass-through/downstream error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the receiver's recorded logs

FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of returning the receiver or a logger sharing its state. LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx) (logger_middleware.go:58), so a test holding the original TestLogger and asserting on InfoLogs will observe zero calls even though a log was emitted; the fake therefore no longer behaves like the real logger (which writes to the same underlying output) and will silently hide the new Plugin Request Completed log in tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers contextual-logger propagation or the LoggerMiddleware field move

The refactor removes the explicit pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname fields from LoggerMiddleware.logRequest and relies entirely on ContextualLoggerMiddleware enriching the context earlier in the chain plus Logger.FromContext honouring it, yet the only renamed test still asserts Prometheus metrics and never checks the context seen downstream or the emitted Plugin Request Completed fields. A regression in middleware ordering or in FromContext (in either the real or fake logger) that drops those log fields would pass the whole suite undetected; a chain-level test for the new middleware is needed.

Streaming endpoints do not receive the contextual logger

SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the original context to next without calling instrumentContext, unlike QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics. These request types also carry a PluginContext, so any logging performed downstream via a contextual logger during streaming (including long-lived RunStream handlers) will lack endpoint, pluginId, dsName/dsUID and uname, making the extracted ContextualLoggerMiddleware incomplete and its behaviour inconsistent across endpoints.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one database session and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction, lock, or database constraint enforcing the maximum row count. Two concurrent requests for different new devices, on the same or different Grafana instances, can both observe count == deviceLimit-1 and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. The per-process local cache does not coordinate distinct device IDs or multiple instances. The count check and admission of a new device need to be made atomic, for example with a locking transaction or another database-enforced mechanism.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected devices are cached and then allowed on the next request

tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache with SetDefault before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and it never evicts that entry when the store returns an error. A new device over the limit therefore fails once with ErrDeviceLimitReached, but its next request on the same instance within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early cache return, TagDevice reports success, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity even though the device was never inserted. Concurrent requests can also observe the cache entry set by an in-flight request that is later rejected. Set the cache only after a successful store write, or delete the entry on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now blocks on device tagging without a timeout

Authenticate previously tagged devices in a goroutine with panic recovery and a two-minute background-context timeout. It now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context and no timeout or recovery. A slow or blocked anon_device count/insert therefore stalls anonymous authentication for the full database/request duration, request cancellation can abort the limit decision, and a panic in tagging now propagates into request authentication instead of merely degrading tagging. Use a bounded context for the now-synchronous enforcement call and preserve appropriate panic handling.

Device-limit tests do not cover allowed updates or the service authentication path

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second distinct device is rejected by the store when the limit is 1. It does not verify the intended complementary behavior that the already-admitted device can still be updated while count >= limit, and no test exercises AnonDeviceService.TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate repeatedly after a rejection. Those missing cases leave both the updateDevice success path and service-level enforcement behaviour unverified. Add tests for updating the existing device at the limit and for repeated service-level requests from a rejected device.

New device_limit setting is absent from shipped configuration definitions

The PR parses auth.anonymous/device_limit into Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit, but it does not add device_limit to conf/defaults.ini, the sample configuration, or the Grafana configuration documentation. Operators therefore cannot discover the new limit from the shipped configuration, and configuration/environment handling that enumerates known keys may not surface it consistently. Add the default and explanatory documentation alongside the existing auth.anonymous settings.

Provider signature changes are not reflected in dependency wiring

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changes its third parameter from anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore in anonstore/database.go additionally changes from accepting only db.DB to requiring an int64 deviceLimit. The checked-in Wire injector/provider wiring that calls these constructors is not updated or regenerated in this PR, so code generated/called with the old arguments no longer compiles and Wire has no ordinary injectable int64 binding for the new store parameter. Update and regenerate the wiring, or keep the store injectable and supply the configured limit through its existing provider wiring.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags unconditionally call r.log.Error before and after every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including successful batches and the final empty batch where err is nil and affected is 0. Normal periodic cleanup will therefore flood error logs, trigger error-based alerting/log pipelines, and serialize ID slices that can contain up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (tested at 32767) entries per batch. These diagnostic messages should be Debug level, should not log the full ID slice, and errors should only be logged/returned when the batch actually fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs without justification

This changes the interval for CleanUpService.Run from 10 minutes to 1 minute. That ticker drives every job in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp-user invites, short URLs, and query-history enforcement will now run 10x as often, increasing database and log load in every Grafana instance. The PR description only justifies splitting the annotation DELETE statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks and does not mention or justify this frequency change, so it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or separately justified and scoped to annotations.

false_positives.candidate:
Parameter-limit workaround only handles SQLite, regressing large batches on other databases

deleteByIDs binds one '?' placeholder per fetched ID for every database except the special-cased SQLite path at lines 608-613. The previous implementation used a subquery DELETE with no per-ID bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable and this PR's own test raises it to 32767; a larger configured batch (over 65535 parameters) will now fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL with bind-parameter limits even though the old statement would have succeeded, aborting cleanup partway. The workaround should be based on len(ids) and the actual database's parameter limit, or IDs should be chunked/inlined for all affected dialects.

SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

For SQLite with batch size over 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of up to batch-size IDs (32767 in the added test, applied repeatedly to annotations and orphaned tags) is O(n^2) in time and allocations and can make large cleanups and the new test very slow. Use strings.Builder (or chunk the deletes) instead of re-formatting the whole string per ID.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts legacy-versus-storage latency and error measurements and, for Delete, creates a high-cardinality kind label containing user object names.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label.
