false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object

Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result

Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. Mode 3 performs legacy writes asynchronously with no completion signal, so those assertions race the background legacy write and can intermittently observe missing or stale legacy playlists even when the implementation eventually succeeds. The mode 3 scenarios need eventual-consistency polling for legacy assertions or a different set of expectations from the synchronous modes.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

Multiple goroutines can concurrently observe a nil entryPointAssetsCache under the read lock, then queue on the write lock at line 48. Because the locked section does not re-check the cache, every queued goroutine re-reads and parses assets-manifest.json, overwrites the cache, and blocks other callers while holding the exclusive lock. A cold-start burst therefore defeats the cache and serializes redundant file I/O. After acquiring the lock, return the cached value when cfg.Env is not Dev and the cache is now populated, while preserving the reload behavior in Dev mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix

The change synchronizes entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so CI running with the race detector has no new coverage for the simultaneous cache-miss/cache-hit path that previously raced. Add a same-package test using a valid temporary assets manifest and a non-Dev configuration that launches multiple concurrent GetWebAssets calls, properly resetting the global cache between tests, and verifies all callers succeed with the expected assets.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic

The helper computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false both inside the if and after it, so the feature toggle has no effect and the logic reads as the opposite of its name. It also unnecessarily dereferences h.features: a reader constructed with nil toggles will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the intended disabled error. Replace this with an explicit unconditional disabled return with a comment, or implement the toggle check without negation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command construction path is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts a raw SQL expression and calls NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. It currently fails only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the stub DB's RunCommands and NewSQLCommand maps that 'not implemented' error to a BadRequest for invalid SQL. The kill switch is therefore not enforced at this entry point, produces a misleading error, and restoring a working DB/parser implementation would remove the only construction barrier on this path even though SQL expressions are supposed to be disabled. Add an explicit disabled check to UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand or remove those constructors while the feature is disabled.

No regression test covers the SQL-expression kill switch

This security change makes the reader reject SQL expressions and makes NewSQLCommand/TablesList/Execute fail through the stub DB, but no _test.go file is changed. Add tests proving that a SQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled through ReadQuery, that the raw-node UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand path cannot construct an executable command, and that Execute returns an error rather than running the query; otherwise a future refactor or DB restoration could silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 vulnerable path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent builds for the same index are no longer serialized

BuildIndex now only locks cacheMu when inserting the finished index, while GetIndex (lines 60-68) only checks the cache and has no in-flight tracking. Two concurrent Search/search-init/watch-event calls for the same not-yet-cached NamespacedResource can therefore both invoke BuildIndex, both run the document builder, and for file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory path at line 97. This can fail with an index-exists/lock error, double-count IndexTenants, leak the overwritten index without Close, or corrupt startup/search behaviour; previously GetIndex blocked on the read lock while a build held the write lock. Per-key in-flight deduplication (or equivalent) is needed, not just a short cache-insert lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock, while BuildIndex now concurrently writes b.cache[key] under the write lock at lines 137-139 (and builds now run in parallel during startup and on-demand). Concurrent map iteration and map write is a Go data race and can trigger a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic or race-detector failures. TotalDocs should snapshot or read the cache under RLock.

false_positives.candidate:
Parallel init workers share the outer err and counter without synchronization

In searchSupport.init, every errgroup worker executes 'totalBatchesIndexed++' and '_, _, err = s.build(...); return err' using variables captured from the enclosing scope. With initWorkers > 1 these are unsynchronized concurrent writes/reads: the race detector will flag them, the indexed count can lose increments, and one namespace's build error can be overwritten by another worker's result before it is returned, so init may report success despite a failed namespace build (or report another worker's error). Each worker should use a local err variable and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

Postgres integration coverage for the changed startup path is disabled

The PR adds an unconditional skip for postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, the integration test that exercises the storage-server target whose initialization this PR moves into NewResourceServer. Skipping it removes CI coverage for exactly the eager-init/startup behaviour on postgres and can hide a postgres-specific startup regression (the comment only says it fails in Drone but works locally). The failure should be diagnosed or tracked with a linked issue rather than silently skipped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New cache test cleans up a literal "alias" IdP instead of the created IdPs

The cleanup registration uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, which binds a resource for an IdP literally named "alias" rather than each created idp-alias-i provider; the same mistake is repeated for idp-alias-20 at line 425. Cleanup will attempt to delete a non-existent provider and leave the twenty-plus created IdPs in the shared test realm, making the test order-dependent and potentially polluting other tests in the class. Capture each created alias in a lambda that deletes that alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-string organizationId collides with the null organization cache key

getForLogin() uses "" as the IdentityProviderListQuery search key when organizationId is null, while a caller-supplied organizationId of "" is also non-null and is kept as "". Under the IdentityProviderStorageProvider contract these are different requests: null means IdPs from any organization, whereas "" is passed through as a specific organization-id search. The cache therefore conflates the two cases, so getForLogin(ORG_ONLY or ALL, "") can return the cached all-organizations result, or the reverse ordering can make a null-organization request reuse an empty/specific-organization result. Use a distinct sentinel that cannot be a supplied organizationId, or include the organizationId in the cache key.

Login-cache test never creates or removes a login-qualified IdP

testCacheIDPForLogin only creates a hideOnLogin IdP and removes a disabled IdP to assert that non-qualifying operations do not invalidate the caches, and it exercises invalidation only through an update that changes login availability. It never creates an enabled login-qualified IdP, nor removes one, after the login caches are populated, so a regression in the new positive invalidation paths in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.create() and remove() would not be caught. Add cases asserting that both operations clear the REALM_ONLY/ORG_ONLY/ALL login caches and that subsequent getForLogin calls return the updated membership.

Update invalidation compares an organization-aware model against the raw updated model

update() obtains the original model through getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA-backed getForLogin result, however, is based on the stored enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC fields and does not exclude IdPs merely because their organization is disabled. Therefore, for an IdP in a disabled organization that currently qualifies in the stored data, changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly to a disqualifying value makes both the wrapped original and the updated model fail getLoginPredicate(), so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() returns without invalidating any login cache. The stale cached ID remains and can reappear when the organization is re-enabled, even though the IdP is now hidden or link-only. The comparison should use the unwrapped stored model/fields rather than the organization-aware isEnabled() view.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle

The CryptoProvider contract for getBouncyCastleProvider() is to return the BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns the provider backing a newly created default-type KeyStore, typically the SUN provider for PKCS12. Callers that use the returned provider for BouncyCastle-specific algorithms, keystore types, or provider-name checks will therefore fail or misidentify the active crypto mode. It should return an actual BouncyCastle provider, return null as the Elytron provider does when BouncyCastle is unavailable, or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods in this class.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New order() method is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a ServiceLoader SPI, but order() was added as an abstract method instead of a default method. Any existing out-of-tree or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls CryptoProvider::order during provider detection, and source implementations or mocks will no longer compile. Adding a default implementation, for example returning 0, would preserve compatibility while allowing built-in providers to declare higher precedence.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default-curve key and only assert round-trip identity

The test creates one EC key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so it does not create P-384 or P-521 keys for ES384/ES512. It then only asserts that concatenated R/S converted to DER and back equals the padded concatenated value, without verifying the DER signature against the public key, comparing it with the original JCA DER signature, or checking the expected curve-specific lengths. Defects in 48/66-byte R/S handling, leading-zero stripping, or the long-form DER length needed for real ES512 signatures can therefore pass undetected. Each algorithm should generate a key on its corresponding curve and verify the reconverted DER signature.

Equal provider orders make selection nondeterministic and silently ignore conflicting providers

Providers are now sorted only by order(), while DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If more than one of them is accidentally present, the previous explicit 'multiple crypto providers' error is replaced by silently choosing whichever ServiceLoader/classpath ordering returns first. This can silently select the non-FIPS provider in a deployment expecting FIPS, and ServiceLoader instantiation can already have run the other providers' constructors and their global Java Security provider registration side effects. Built-in providers need distinct priorities or ties at the highest order should remain an error.

Malformed zero-length ASN.1 integer escapes as NumberFormatException instead of IOException

readInteger() passes the decoded byte array directly to new BigInteger(bytes). A malformed DER integer with length 0 makes that constructor throw NumberFormatException, although callers such as asn1derToConcatenatedRS() are written to handle IOException for invalid signatures. Invalid input can consequently abort processing with an unchecked exception instead of the declared, handled error type. Zero-length and otherwise invalid integer encodings should be rejected with IOException before constructing the BigInteger.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients never receive the new Clients type or scopes

init() returns immediately whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. A realm that already enabled FGAP V2 for Users therefore keeps the old resource server, which has no 'Clients' all-resource and lacks the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Creating Clients permissions using those scopes then fails when their scopes cannot be found, and all-clients evaluation has no 'Clients' resource to evaluate, so the new Clients support does not work on already-initialized realms until the admin-permissions client is somehow recreated.

Global canView does not include an all-clients MANAGE grant

canView() only checks the default role-based view check or an FGAP VIEW grant on the all-clients resource. A caller granted only MANAGE on all clients passes canManage() and canView(ClientModel) for each client (through canConfigure/canManage), and canView(ClientScopeModel) explicitly accepts MANAGE, but fails the no-argument canView(). Endpoints that gate on requireView()/canViewClientScopes()/canList-style global checks therefore return 403 for a manage-only administrator who is otherwise allowed to manage and view every client.

Map-roles checks ignore manage permission and manage-clients admins

canMapRoles(), canMapCompositeRoles(), and canMapClientScopeRoles() only check their exact FGAP scope for the client. Unlike canConfigure(), which first delegates to canManage(client), they do not treat a caller with the MANAGE_CLIENTS admin role or an FGAP manage grant on that client (or on all clients) as able to map roles. Such a full client administrator can create, update, configure, and delete the client but is denied client role-mapping and composite-role operations under V2, breaking role administration for otherwise fully privileged admins.

Removal listener still dispatches to V2 when both FGAP features are enabled

The new guard only checks ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1), but AdminPermissions.management() selects MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, regardless of V1. With both features enabled, a ClientRemovedEvent therefore calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(), which unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException, instead of the V1 cleanup the listener intends to run. The guard needs to exclude the V2 case, e.g. run only when V1 is enabled and V2 is not.

getResourceName has no Clients branch

getResourceName() special-cases only the Users resource type, translating a user resource id to the username and the Users all-resource to 'All users'. Client resources fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for resources created by getOrCreateResource() is the client UUID, and the Clients all-resource is not labelled 'All clients'. Permission and resource representations for the new Clients type will therefore show opaque client UUIDs instead of the clientId, unlike the human-readable names provided for Users.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Caution incorrectly implies all operator deployments fail without rolling-updates

The added caution says that while in preview the rolling-updates feature must be enabled, otherwise the Keycloak Operator will fail. As written this is unconditional, but the same section documents '<not set>' as the default strategy that mimics Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior, which is a supported configuration that does not opt into the new update-strategy handling. Readers running the operator without spec.update.strategy will conclude they must enable a preview feature or their existing deployment will break. Scope the caution to deployments that actually use the update feature/strategy (for example when spec.update.strategy is set), mirroring whatever the operator really requires.

Default-strategy deployments are created without the required rolling-updates feature

createInitialDeployment() returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before enabling Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES. Both parameterized tests use the null/default strategy: testCacheMaxCount expects a rolling upgrade for the null case, and testImageChange also exercises the operator upgrade flow. The PR's own operator documentation states that the rolling-updates feature must be enabled or the operator will fail, and the CLI check now exits with FEATURE_DISABLED when it is not enabled. The null-strategy cases therefore either fail/recreate instead of rolling or are not actually testing the new feature-gated path. Enable rolling-updates for the default case as well, or explicitly document and adjust the expectations if the default path is exempt.

New exit-code contract for disabled feature and recreate is not asserted

This PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and introduces FEATURE_DISABLED=4, while the guide tells users to rely only on the check command's exit code. However testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the metadata subcommand and only asserts the stderr text; it does not assert exit code 4, and there is no equivalent disabled-feature test for the check subcommand. testWrongVersions likewise asserts messages but not exit code 3. A regression that swaps or breaks these codes would therefore pass the tests while breaking scripts and the operator that consume the numeric codes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW permission on all groups grants global group manage

canManage() with no group argument returns true for either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource. This method backs GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup via requireManage(), so an FGAP admin granted only view access to all groups can create top-level groups and perform other global manage operations. Unlike canManage(GroupModel), which correctly requires only MANAGE, the global check should require MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

Group authorization resources are created with the group ID as the resource name, while Resource.getId() is an unrelated internal authorization-store UUID. This loop calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...), which does findByName(server, UUID) and therefore misses the per-group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource, and then adds that same UUID to the granted set. Callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser and getUsersCount expect actual GroupModel IDs in UserModel.GROUPS, so per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are not correctly used to filter or count group members. It should pass and return groupResource.getName() and must not treat the all-groups type resource (named 'Groups') as a group.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAP v2 realms never receive the new Groups resource or scopes

init() returns immediately whenever the realm already has an admin-permissions client. Realms that enabled FGAP v2 before this change therefore keep a resource server containing only the previously defined Clients and Users all-type resources and scopes, with no Groups resource and no manage-members/view-members/manage-membership scopes. Group permissions cannot be created or evaluated correctly in such realms; GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission can also receive null from getResourceTypeResource and pass it to policyStore.findByResource. The schema initialization needs an upgrade path that adds missing resource types and scopes for an existing admin-permissions client, or evaluation needs null-safe handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 was replaced with Italian text

The Lithuanian account message totpStep1 now reads "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian, replacing the previous Lithuanian sentence. Lithuanian users will see setup instructions in the wrong language. Replace it with a Lithuanian translation of "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:" without the removed anchor tags.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese file now uses Traditional Chinese text

The new totpStep1 text "在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：" uses Traditional Chinese characters (手機, 應用程式) in the messages_zh_CN (Simplified Chinese) file. It should use the Simplified Chinese equivalent, e.g. "在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：", to match the locale.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor mismatch error does not identify the file or key

santizeAnchors() receives the message key but never uses it, and the added message only says "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string". Unlike the Illegal HTML message, it contains neither the key nor the file. When the verifier runs over hundreds of properties files and thousands of keys, a translator cannot locate the offending entry from this message. Include the key and file in the anchor-mismatch message.

HTML inside MessageFormat choice branches is never sanitized

normalizeValue() replaces each complete {n,choice,...} expression with "..." before the OWASP sanitizer runs. Consequently, markup placed in a choice branch for keys such as linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit.* or error-invalid-multivalued-size is never inspected: for example a branch containing a script or malicious anchor passes verification if the rest of the value passes, but MessageFormat can select and output that branch at runtime. The verifier should check the text of each choice alternative after removing only the choice syntax and comparison operators, rather than discarding the whole expression.

Java MessageFormat choice syntax breaks Account UI interpolation

This Account UI resource uses i18next-style double-brace placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, etc.) throughout the file, but error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed to Java MessageFormat syntax: {0}, {1}, and {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}. i18next does not evaluate MessageFormat choice expressions, so this value will render literal or unresolved placeholders instead of the interpolated limits and pluralized noun. Keep the UI resource in its double-brace/value(s) form and handle that form in the verifier instead.

Java MessageFormat choice syntax breaks Admin UI interpolation

As in the other React UI resources, this file previously used i18next-style {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} placeholders for error-invalid-multivalued-size, but it was changed to Java MessageFormat {0}/{1}/{2,choice,...}. The Admin UI's i18next interpolation does not evaluate MessageFormat choice expressions, so the formatted error can show literal placeholders instead of the attribute limits. The Java choice form belongs only in the server-side theme properties, not in this UI resource.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 was replaced with Italian text

The Lithuanian login message loginTotpStep1 now reads "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian, replacing the previous Lithuanian sentence. Lithuanian users will see TOTP setup instructions in the wrong language during login. Replace it with the Lithuanian translation of the anchor-free English sentence.

Missing English counterpart aborts verification with an unchecked exception

verifySafeHtml() derives the English file by rewriting the locale suffix and throws a raw RuntimeException if that derived file cannot be read. verify() only converts IOException to MojoExecutionException and callers otherwise receive collected message strings, so a properties file without a matching _en counterpart (or with a differently named English locale) aborts the whole verification run and masks all other results instead of producing a locatable verification/build error for that file.

No positive test that legitimate HTML and anchors pass verification

All new sanitizer tests assert that violations are reported; none asserts an empty result for a valid translation that uses allowed HTML (p/strong/b/br) when the English source contains HTML, or for a translation reusing the exact English anchor. A regression that strips or flags all allowed markup, or breaks the anchor-removal logic so legitimate translations always fail, would still pass this suite. Add clean English/translation fixtures expecting no messages.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId

The fourth constructor check is Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed"), repeating the grantType check instead of checking the rawTokenId parameter. A null rawTokenId therefore slips through and encodeTokenId() silently produces an ID ending in ':null', which later decodes to the literal raw ID "null" rather than failing fast at construction.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong substring and inverts the comparison

The encoded token ID format is two chars session type, two chars token type, then two chars grant type, so the grant shortcut is items[0].substring(4, 6). The matcher uses substring(3, 5) and returns false when that substring equals expectedGrantShortcut. For a normal ID such as onrtac the checked substring is 'ta', never 'ac', so expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken pass regardless of the encoded grant type as long as the raw part is a UUID; the new grant-encoding behaviour is effectively untested by these integration assertions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcut length is documented inconsistently and never validated

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() javadoc describes the value as 'usually like 3-letters', but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider encodes session, token and grant shortcuts without validating length and getTokenContextFromTokenId() requires the whole encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters, i.e. exactly 2 characters per shortcut. A factory following the javadoc and returning a 3-letter shortcut, or returning a 1-letter/empty/null shortcut, produces token IDs that the decoder rejects, or fails with an NPE from the ConcurrentHashMap, instead of being rejected clearly at startup. Document exactly two characters and validate uniqueness and length in postInit() and in the lazy refresh paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Decoding throws on malformed or newer token IDs instead of returning UNKNOWN

getTokenContextFromTokenId() returns UNKNOWN for legacy token IDs without a colon, but throws IllegalArgumentException for any colon-containing ID whose prefix is not exactly 6 characters or whose session/token/grant shortcut is unknown to this node. That is inconsistent backward-compatibility handling: during rolling upgrades, or when the planned introspection/userinfo consumers decode tokens issued by a newer node with a new shortcut, validation would fail with an exception rather than falling back to the normal session lookup. Unknown or malformed encodings should be treated like legacy IDs and return UNKNOWN context.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks custom grant-type factories

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an extension interface, but getShortcut() was added as an abstract method without a default implementation. Existing custom grant factories compiled against the old interface will fail with AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(), and source implementations will no longer compile. This can break server startup or token issuance for deployments with custom grants. Provide a default implementation, for example returning the unknown shortcut, so existing factories continue to work.

Public OAuth2GrantType.Context copy constructor was removed

The previously public Context(Context) copy constructor has been removed while changing the main constructor to derive grantType from formParams. Code in custom grant types or delegating/wrapping grant implementations that used new OAuth2GrantType.Context(existingContext) will now fail to compile, and already-compiled code will fail with NoSuchMethodError. The copy constructor should be retained, copying grantType as well, or at least deprecated through a compatibility cycle.

Unknown grant type now fails all access-token issuance instead of falling back

TokenManager.initToken() calls encodeTokenId() for every access token, and encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException when the GRANT_TYPE client-session attribute is a non-null value that is not exactly a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory id. The deassign suppression uses separate branches in GroupAssignee.deassign and in sync_group_assignee_inbound's assign=False path, so a regression there would still echo unassignments back to the originating integration and would not be caught. There is also no test that an assignment sourced from one integration still syncs to a different linked integration, so over-suppression would not be caught either.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Rebalanced strategy reuses an irreversibly shut-down queue pool

The factory creates FixedQueuePool once during construction, while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts that pool down. Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory when partitions are revoked and reassigned, so the new strategy receives workers that have exited and queues on which shutdown() has already been called. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that exception and marks the offset complete, allowing messages to be committed without being processed. A normal Kafka rebalance can therefore cause silent data loss until the process is restarted.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs an exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can consequently commit the offset for a result that was never successfully handled, contradicting the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing and causing failed uptime results to be lost rather than redelivered.

Unbounded queues provide no Arroyo backpressure

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and therefore has no maximum size, and submit() never raises MessageRejected or otherwise blocks. If workers process more slowly than Kafka delivers, Arroyo can continue submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory use and hiding the backlog from Kafka flow control. This also makes the class documentation's claim of natural backpressure when queues fill up incorrect because these queues never fill.

Close stops offset committing before workers finish and shutdown drops queued work

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() stops and joins the commit thread before shutting down the queue pool, so results completed by workers afterward have no commit loop left to commit their offsets and will be redelivered. In addition, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False); a busy worker exits after its current item instead of draining its queue. Graceful close therefore both leaves processed offsets uncommitted and abandons queued work rather than finishing it within the strategy's join period.

Python's salted hash does not provide consistent group-to-queue assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() for a string group key. Python randomizes string hashing per interpreter unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed, so the same subscription can map to different queues after a restart or when processed by another consumer process. That undermines the documented consistent-assignment and per-group ordering guarantee across rebalances and deployments; a stable digest such as hashlib.md5 or sha256 should be used instead.

Invalid max_workers values are silently accepted for thread-queue-parallel mode

The CLI accepts any integer for --max-workers, and this code converts 0 to 20 with 'or' while passing a negative value through as num_queues. A negative value creates no queues or workers; submissions then fail with an index/modulo error, are caught by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), and are marked complete, so their offsets can be committed without processing. The option should be validated as a positive integer before constructing the pool.

Blocked offsets make commit checks repeatedly scan an ever-growing set

OffsetTracker retains every offset after a blocked or very slow offset, because offsets can only be removed after a contiguous commit. get_committable_offsets() is called once per second and computes both min() and max() over that retained set each time. During exactly the slow-item backlog this feature is meant to tolerate, the set can grow to a large number of completed offsets and the commit loop becomes repeated O(n) work while also retaining unbounded tracking state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets are passed to Django queryset slicing, which does not support them

Cursor values and offsets come from the request query string and Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets. The optimized branch deliberately uses cursor.offset as the slice start when enable_advanced_features is set, and BasePaginator at line 182 likewise preserves negative offsets for is_prev cursors. The claim that Django ORM handles this is false: Django QuerySet slicing asserts 'Negative indexing is not supported', so a crafted cursor such as a negative-offset prev/next cursor produces a 500 rather than safely paging from the end. Pagination bounds need explicit validation/clamping before slicing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact bug described in the golden comment: passing negative cursor offsets to Django queryset slicing in the optimized branch when enable_advanced_features is set.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that BasePaginator preserves negative offsets for is_prev cursors and passes them to Django queryset slicing without clamping, which matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime ordering of its only caller

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key), and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer. Its only caller orders AuditLogEntry by -datetime, for which DateTimePaginator is required: it converts epoch-millis cursor values to timezone-aware datetimes and formats item keys with strftime. With -datetime, build_queryset receives an integer instead of a datetime and build_cursor calls math.floor on a datetime, so the optimized audit-log path will raise TypeError/database comparison errors instead of returning a page.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on a datetime object because the caller orders by '-datetime', which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Unrelated audit-log change enables unvetted advanced pagination for non-superusers

This spans-buffer PR also switches the audit-log endpoint to OptimizedCursorPaginator when optimized_pagination=true is supplied and the caller is a superuser OR merely has organization_context.member.has_global_access. has_global_access is team-access scope for ordinary organization members, not proof of administrator/superuser status as the comment claims. This exposes a separate, user-controlled pagination implementation on a sensitive endpoint, unrelated to span buffering, and should be removed or reviewed/tested as its own API change.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts span end-timestamp scores on overlaps

The old SUNIONSTORE deduplicated identical payloads without changing metadata. The new redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key) uses Redis' default AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both sorted sets (duplicate delivery, a merge of overlapping partial segments, or destination/source overlap) gets score roughly end_timestamp+end_timestamp instead of its end timestamp. That corrupts the score later used by zpopmin eviction, artificially protecting duplicated spans and causing other spans to be evicted first. Use an explicit AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve one real timestamp.

SET-to-ZSET switch breaks in-flight Redis segments with WRONGTYPE errors

Existing buffered segment keys were created as Redis SETs by sadd and can remain live until the one-hour redis_ttl/flush timeouts expire. This change immediately issues ZADD in process_spans, and the Lua script likewise issues ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN, while flush uses ZSCAN. Redis returns WRONGTYPE when a sorted-set command is used on an existing SET key, so during rollout process_spans fails for traces already buffered, batches retry/stall, and unflushed spans can be lost when the old keys expire. The PR contains no key versioning, drain, dual-type handling, or other migration for in-flight keys.

Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed while insert cap ignores the configured limit

_load_segment_data no longer enforces SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans; after this change that constructor setting is effectively dead. Eviction is instead hardcoded to 1000 in add-buffer.lua, so the default changes from 1001 to 1000 and any custom max_segment_spans value is silently ignored. Segments that bypass insert eviction, including pre-existing large segments, are now loaded and emitted regardless of span count, bounded only by max_segment_bytes, increasing memory and downstream segment-size risk.

Redirect resolution depth silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop previously allowed 10000 hops, with a comment acknowledging that deeper segment trees might not be joined correctly. Reducing it to 1000 makes that failure mode ten times more likely: when the cap is exhausted the script proceeds with an unresolved set_span_id and no error, so spans for a deep chain can be placed in a different segment key and flushed as split/incomplete segments rather than being joined to their root segment.

Insert-time eviction silently drops spans with no metric or truncation signal

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin permanently discards the earliest-ending spans during insert. Unlike the removed flush-time span-count guard, which emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded and logged the segment size, this path emits no metric/log and marks the flushed segment in no way as truncated. Operators cannot measure span loss and downstream consumers receive an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one.

No test covers the new eviction, sorted-set merge, or score behavior

The test changes only add the newly required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment, asserts which spans zpopmin retains, covers duplicate payloads across merged partial segments, or verifies that scores remain real end timestamps after ZUNIONSTORE. The central data-loss behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset instead of the dataset actually being queried

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which is the dataset that will execute the query, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable dataset from the request. The dashboard-split factory calls _get_event_stats with different datasets, including discover for error splits and the scoped dataset for transaction-like splits. Consequently, an error split can incorrectly miss upsampling, while a metrics or transaction-like query can receive upsampled_count() even though that builder or table does not support sample_weight. The decision should be based on scoped_dataset and the query actually being executed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset` (the dataset actually executing the query), which causes incorrect upsampling behavior during dashboard splits.

false_positives.candidate:
Error-focus detection ignores the actual query and uses a naive substring check

The transform decision reads only request.GET['query'] and checks whether it contains 'event.type:error'. _get_event_stats is not given the opportunity to pass its query argument, which may be an internally constructed dashboard query such as '(...) AND !event.type:transaction' or a widget query that differs from the request parameter. The substring check also misses forms such as '!event.type:transaction' and 'event.type:[error, default]', while incorrectly matching the negated query '!event.type:error'. Error charts can therefore remain unupsampled, or non-error queries can have count() replaced by a sum of sample_weight.

upsampled_count has no fallback for missing sample weights and truncates fractional weights

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested before error sampling was enabled, or that otherwise have a null or zero sample_weight, contribute nothing instead of counting as one event, so historical and unsampled errors disappear from upsampled series. Additionally, toInt64 truncates fractional sums produced by float sample weights, systematically undercounting estimated errors. Missing weights should default to 1 and the fractional estimate should be rounded or retained rather than truncated.

Internal upsampled_count function is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike neighboring internal-only aggregation helpers. It therefore expands the public Discover function surface and can be requested directly through query builders using DiscoverDatasetConfig, bypassing the stats endpoint's project-allowlist and dataset checks. On non-allowlisted projects or datasets backed by tables without meaningful error sample weights, this can return misleading counts or produce invalid Snuba queries. The function should remain internal to the gated transformation.

Cached allowlist eligibility can remain stale and the invalidation helper is never used

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds, but invalidate_upsampling_cache has no caller in this change and there is no hook from option changes to that helper. After a project is removed from issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist, the endpoint can continue replacing count() with upsampled counts; after a project is added, it can continue returning raw counts until the entry expires. Either wire invalidation to allowlist changes or remove the unused invalidation API and explicitly accept only TTL-based expiry.

Stray subproject file is unrelated to the feature

This change adds a root-level 'sentry-repo' file containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a'. That resembles an accidentally recorded nested-repository gitlink without any corresponding submodule configuration and is unrelated to error upsampling. It can confuse checkout and submodule tooling and should be removed before merging.

Tests do not exercise the public eligibility entry point used by the endpoint

The unit tests import and test only the private helpers _are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, and the column transform. They do not test is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, the only function called by organization_events_stats, including its caching behavior, dataset handling, or interaction with a scoped/split dataset. The Snuba tests also cover only events that already carry client_sample_rate=0.1, leaving unsampled events and the resulting sample_weight behavior unverified, so regressions in the actual production path can pass the added tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored

The test named "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}; despite the comment saying this allows access, checkPermission treats a false map value as no permission, and the fake permission store also returns no granting permission. The request therefore denies through the ordinary cached/DB path even if permDenialCache is never consulted, so the test does not prove the new short-circuit works. It should configure the underlying store or permission cache to allow dash1, or assert that the permission store is not called when the denial entry is present.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same flaw in the test as the golden comment: the test sets the cached permission map value for 'dashboards:uid:dash1' to false instead of true, contradicting the comment that says it 'allows access' and causing checkPermission to deny access regardless of the denial cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous

userPermDenialCacheKey joins variable-length UID, action, name, and parent values with plain underscores and no escaping, length prefixes, or hashing. Distinct tuples can consequently produce the same key: for example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. Grafana resource and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny a different resource until the entry expires. Build the key from a structured, unambiguously encoded or hashed tuple.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using plain underscore concatenation without escaping or length prefixing, which leads to key collisions and incorrect permission denial cache hits when components contain underscores.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include the identity type

The denial key is built only from namespace, the raw subject UID, action, resource name, and parent folder, but permission resolution switches on identity type and returns different permission sets for the same UID. In particular, anonymous and render-service subjects both use UID "0", while anonymous receives Viewer-role permissions and the render service is granted read access to all dashboards and folders. A denial recorded for anonymous:0 can therefore short-circuit and incorrectly deny render:0 for the same dashboard for up to the denial TTL, and the same collision can occur between user and service-account spellings. The key must include the identity type, preferably together with the canonical resolved UID.

Denial entries shadow fresher permissions and undermine immediate access after a grant

Check consults permDenialCache before checking the ordinary permission cache, and neither getUserPermissions' permission-cache refresh nor List's refresh deletes existing denial entries. After a permission is granted, such as the creator permission inserted for a new dashboard or folder, a later check or list for another resource can refresh permCache with a scope map that now allows the denied resource, yet checks for that resource will still return the old denial until the denial TTL expires. A denial recorded by a check made just before the grant has the same effect. This partially defeats the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created resources immediately; cached allowances should be honoured before denials or denials should be invalidated when permissions are refreshed.

Every distinct cached denial now forces a database permission fetch

When cached permissions do not allow a check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the permission-store cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so this performs a fresh database permission query. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent tuple for 30 seconds. A user checking many distinct dashboards or folders they do not own therefore causes one permission query per resource instead of one query per user/action as before, multiplying database load in denial-heavy or enumeration-heavy workloads and increasing cache cardinality. The revalidation needs a freshness or negative-cache strategy that does not scale database queries with the number of distinct denied resources.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender check raises KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata

The check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. Integrations created through the normal pipeline only get metadata["sender"] when state happens to contain a sender (the updated test's basic flow asserts metadata with no sender key), and integrations created before sender tracking existed likewise lack it. When such an Integration exists but its OrganizationIntegration has been removed, this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of either proceeding or showing the integration-failed page, breaking reinstallation/moving of those integrations. The lookup should use a safe .get() chain and define the behavior when sender is absent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: unconditionally accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` will raise a `KeyError` for integrations where the `sender` key is missing in metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not exist yet

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the Integration.DoesNotExist branch immediately returns pipeline.next_step(), while the github_authenticated_user versus integration.metadata["sender"] comparison at lines 500-505 only runs when an Integration already exists without an OrganizationIntegration. A newly installed GitHub App therefore completes without any sender check if the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration row (a normal race, since GitHub sends the webhook and the user redirect independently) or if the webhook was missed/delayed. An attacker who installed the app can have a different Sentry user claim that installation_id during that window, defeating the validation this PR is intended to add; the check needs to fail closed or obtain the installer identity from a source available at build_integration/finish time rather than relying solely on a pre-existing row.

Token-exchange network errors escape the graceful error handling

OAuthLoginView calls safe_urlopen() before the try block; only safe_urlread()/decoding/parsing is wrapped. If GitHub's access-token endpoint is unreachable, resets the connection, or safe_urlopen rejects/errors on the request, the exception propagates as an unhandled 500 instead of rendering the github-integration-failed page that the PR promises for a failed code exchange. The safe_urlopen call (and the unguarded get_user_info call that follows) should be covered by the same failure path that handles a missing access_token.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The rewritten test supplies state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which does not match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView returns the generic invalid-request page before build_integration/get_installation_info is ever reached. The test therefore passes even if the GitHub 404 handling ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') is broken or removed, and it silently drops the previous coverage/assertion for that message. The test should drive the flow with the correct pipeline state and an installation_id step so the mocked 404 from /app/installations/{id} is what produces the failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New cache test cleans up a literal "alias" IdP instead of the created IdPs

The cleanup registration uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, which binds a resource for an IdP literally named "alias" rather than each created idp-alias-i provider; the same mistake is repeated for idp-alias-20 at line 425. Cleanup will attempt to delete a non-existent provider and leave the twenty-plus created IdPs in the shared test realm, making the test order-dependent and potentially polluting other tests in the class. Capture each created alias in a lambda that deletes that alias.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the test cleanup is referencing a hardcoded 'alias' string instead of the dynamically generated 'idp-alias-' + i.

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation compares an organization-aware model against the raw updated model

update() obtains the original model through getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA-backed getForLogin result, however, is based on the stored enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC fields and does not exclude IdPs merely because their organization is disabled. Therefore, for an IdP in a disabled organization that currently qualifies in the stored data, changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly to a disqualifying value makes both the wrapped original and the updated model fail getLoginPredicate(), so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() returns without invalidating any login cache. The stale cached ID remains and can reappear when the organization is re-enabled, even though the IdP is now hidden or link-only. The comparison should use the unwrapped stored model/fields rather than the organization-aware isEnabled() view.

Empty-string organizationId collides with the null organization cache key

getForLogin() uses "" as the IdentityProviderListQuery search key when organizationId is null, while a caller-supplied organizationId of "" is also non-null and is kept as "". Under the IdentityProviderStorageProvider contract these are different requests: null means IdPs from any organization, whereas "" is passed through as a specific organization-id search. The cache therefore conflates the two cases, so getForLogin(ORG_ONLY or ALL, "") can return the cached all-organizations result, or the reverse ordering can make a null-organization request reuse an empty/specific-organization result. Use a distinct sentinel that cannot be a supplied organizationId, or include the organizationId in the cache key.

Login-cache test never creates or removes a login-qualified IdP

testCacheIDPForLogin only creates a hideOnLogin IdP and removes a disabled IdP to assert that non-qualifying operations do not invalidate the caches, and it exercises invalidation only through an update that changes login availability. It never creates an enabled login-qualified IdP, nor removes one, after the login caches are populated, so a regression in the new positive invalidation paths in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.create() and remove() would not be caught. Add cases asserting that both operations clear the REALM_ONLY/ORG_ONLY/ALL login caches and that subsequent getForLogin calls return the updated membership.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic

The helper computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false both inside the if and after it, so the feature toggle has no effect and the logic reads as the opposite of its name. It also unnecessarily dereferences h.features: a reader constructed with nil toggles will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the intended disabled error. Replace this with an explicit unconditional disabled return with a comment, or implement the toggle check without negation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the enableSqlExpressions function contains flawed logic that causes it to unconditionally return false, disabling SQL expressions.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy SQL command construction path is not explicitly disabled

UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts a raw SQL expression and calls NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. It currently fails only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the stub DB's RunCommands and NewSQLCommand maps that 'not implemented' error to a BadRequest for invalid SQL. The kill switch is therefore not enforced at this entry point, produces a misleading error, and restoring a working DB/parser implementation would remove the only construction barrier on this path even though SQL expressions are supposed to be disabled. Add an explicit disabled check to UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand or remove those constructors while the feature is disabled.

No regression test covers the SQL-expression kill switch

This security change makes the reader reject SQL expressions and makes NewSQLCommand/TablesList/Execute fail through the stub DB, but no _test.go file is changed. Add tests proving that a SQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled through ReadQuery, that the raw-node UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand path cannot construct an executable command, and that Execute returns an error rather than running the query; otherwise a future refactor or DB restoration could silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 vulnerable path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

Multiple goroutines can concurrently observe a nil entryPointAssetsCache under the read lock, then queue on the write lock at line 48. Because the locked section does not re-check the cache, every queued goroutine re-reads and parses assets-manifest.json, overwrites the cache, and blocks other callers while holding the exclusive lock. A cold-start burst therefore defeats the cache and serializes redundant file I/O. After acquiring the lock, return the cached value when cfg.Env is not Dev and the cache is now populated, while preserving the reload behavior in Dev mode.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where the cache is checked under a read lock, but not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing redundant cache population by concurrent goroutines.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix

The change synchronizes entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so CI running with the race detector has no new coverage for the simultaneous cache-miss/cache-hit path that previously raced. Add a same-package test using a valid temporary assets manifest and a non-Dev configuration that launches multiple concurrent GetWebAssets calls, properly resetting the global cache between tests, and verifies all callers succeed with the expected assets.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
