false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object

Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result

Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. Mode 3 performs legacy writes asynchronously with no completion signal, so those assertions race the background legacy write and can intermittently observe missing or stale legacy playlists even when the implementation eventually succeeds. The mode 3 scenarios need eventual-consistency polling for legacy assertions or a different set of expectations from the synchronous modes.

runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target here, but splitQueriesByStreamShard (line 163) then passes those targets to runSplitQuery, which at querySplitting.ts:299 calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables again for every shard/time sub-request; the updated shard test even expects 5 applyTemplateVariables calls for one original query. Loki's applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters adhoc filters into the stream selector and re-runs template replacement, neither of which is guaranteed idempotent: repeated passes can add the same adhoc matcher again and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by a first-pass variable value, besides re-parsing already-interpolated LogQL per chunk. Interpolation should be owned by one layer, e.g. the shard layer should be able to tell runSplitQuery its targets are already interpolated.

Split queries are interpolated again by datasource.runQuery for every chunk

The queries interpolated here are built into grouped sub-requests and executed via datasource.runQuery in runSplitGroupedQueries (line 180). Loki's runQuery backend path (DataSourceWithBackend.query) applies applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and request.filters before sending each chunk to the backend, so every split query is now interpolated at least twice, and three times on the shard path. As with the shard double-interpolation, the repeated adhoc-filter injection from request.filters and repeated templateSrv replacement of already-substituted values are not guaranteed idempotent and can corrupt or invalidly duplicate stream-selector matchers. The early interpolation for splitting decisions needs to be reconciled with the downstream one, rather than simply adding another pass.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded on the translation path

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale), while ApplicationController#set_locale is the only caller of I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Code outside a web request, such as background jobs and mailers, and translations using an explicit locale: option can therefore invoke the new Fallbacks backend before the site-default and :en YAML files have been lazily loaded. Those lookups return 'translation missing' instead of falling back; for calls without interpolation arguments, that missing string is also stored frozen in the LRU cache keyed only by key and locale, so it can continue to be served after a later request loads :en until cache eviction or reload. All fallback locales for the effective or explicit locale should be loaded inside translate/lookup before consulting or caching the backend.

Custom fallbacks object discards I18n::Locale::Fallbacks behavior

FallbackLocaleList inherits directly from Hash and replaces the I18n::Locale::Fallbacks object previously configured by Rails, but its [] ignores anything stored in the hash and the class provides neither Locale::Fallbacks' defaults nor its map configuration API. It also loses parent-tag expansion: for a locale such as en_GB, a missing key is resolved in SiteSetting.default_locale before its parent :en, because :en appears only as the final entry. Existing or plugin code using the documented fallbacks API can therefore be silently ignored or fail, and regional locales can receive the site language instead of their parent language. The custom ordering should be implemented by subclassing or extending I18n::Locale::Fallbacks rather than replacing it with a plain Hash.

Every backend lookup now consults SiteSetting

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] for every uncached translation, localization, and pluralization lookup, and this implementation calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every such call. That puts the DB-backed settings subsystem on the hot translation path that translate_accelerator otherwise optimizes through lazy loading and caching, and it also makes translations attempted during boot, rake, or asset tasks depend on SiteSetting being loadable before the fallback chain can even be computed. The chain should be cached and invalidated when default_locale changes, rather than recomputed through SiteSetting for each lookup.

No tests cover the custom fallback backend or lazy loading

This change replaces the Rails fallback configuration with a custom Hash, moves pluralization setup into config/initializers/i18n.rb, removes config.i18n.fallbacks from the environment files, and adds lazy loading of fallback locales, but it adds no specs. Nothing verifies that a key missing from the user locale falls back first to the site default and then to :en, that the relevant locale files are loaded outside ApplicationController, or that pluralized strings obtained through a fallback still use the fallback locale's pluralization rules. Regressions would surface only as wrong-language text or 'translation missing' strings in production.

Legacy embeddable_hosts values are inserted with raw SQL instead of going through EmbeddableHost, so the model's before_validation stripping of scheme and path never runs. Values previously accepted and handled by SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host? such as 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234' are stored verbatim, while EmbeddableHost.record_for_host compares lower(host) against URI(referer).host (e.g. 'discourse.org'), so those migrated hosts will never be allowed after the upgrade and embedding silently breaks for them. The unescaped interpolation of h into the INSERT also breaks the migration if a stored value contains a single quote. Normalize (and safely quote/bind) each host before inserting it.
true_positives.reasoning: While the candidate issue primarily focuses on missing host normalization in a migration, it also explicitly identifies the exact same underlying problem as the golden comment: unescaped interpolation of `h` into the SQL INSERT statement, and recommends safely quoting or binding each host.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the legacy embed_category setting was never persisted

The migration dereferences execute(...)[0]['id'] for a query joining site_settings to categories on the embed_category setting. Site settings that were never customized are not stored as rows, so for the common case where embed_category was never set this query returns zero rows, [0] is nil, and nil['id'] raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and the deploy/upgrade. The fallback on lines 14-16 makes the same assumption about an uncategorized_category_id row existing. The migration must handle missing rows (e.g. check cmd_tuples / nil before indexing) and fall back safely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the migration accesses `execute(...)[0]['id']` without checking if any rows were returned, which causes a crash when the `embed_category` setting does not exist in the database.

false_positives.candidate:
Host format validation is inconsistent with host lookup and rejects valid hosts

The format regex allows an optional port (:[0-9]{1,5}), but record_for_host looks up URI(host).host, which strips the port, so a saved host like 'example.com:8080' can never equal the stored string and will never be allowed or assigned a category. Conversely the regex restricts the TLD to 2-5 letters, rejecting valid embed hosts the old free-form setting accepted, such as example.museum or example.technology. Validation, storage normalization, and lookup need to agree on ports and TLD length.

No uniqueness constraint on host makes the host-to-category mapping ambiguous

Nothing prevents duplicate host rows: the model has no uniqueness validation and the migration creates the table without a unique index. An admin can create the same host twice with different categories, after which record_for_host's unordered .first picks an arbitrary row, so topics imported from that host are filed into a nondeterministic category and host_allowed?/category behavior depends on database row order. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness validation and a unique database index (after normalizing case in storage).

Clicking edit crashes when the host has no resolved category

The edit action does this.get('host.category.id') without checking that category exists. A host's category is undefined when its category was deleted, and also right after saving a new host without choosing a category: save() sets category from Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')) with a null categoryId while the server silently defaults to the uncategorized category, leaving host.category undefined in the client. Clicking the pencil then throws a TypeError and the row can no longer be edited until a page reload. Guard the lookup (host.category && host.category.id) and set the client category to what the server actually assigned.

New admin endpoints have no behavioral test coverage

The specs for Admin::EmbeddableHostsController and Admin::EmbeddingController only assert that the classes inherit from Admin::AdminController. None of the new behavior is exercised: create/update success and validation failure, the blank-category fallback to the uncategorized category in save_host, destroy, or the embedding show payload with its hosts. Regressions in these endpoints (including the nil-record handling) would not be caught. Add request/controller specs covering those paths for a logged-in admin.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is off by one when member count is an exact multiple of the page size

totalPages computes Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. For user_count=50 and limit=50 this returns 2 instead of 1, and for 100/50 it returns 3 instead of 2. showingLast therefore stays false on the real last page, the Next link stays enabled, and clicking it loads an empty page at offset == user_count. It should use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) (with the existing zero-count special case).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same pagination bug where having a total user count equal to a multiple of the limit allows navigating to an empty page (e.g., page 2/2 with offset == user_count). While the golden comment points to the next offset capping and the candidate points to the totalPages calculation that enables the next button, they are describing the same underlying logical flaw and exact same user-facing symptom.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page now silently truncates to the first 50 members with no way to reach the rest

The members endpoint now defaults to limit=50 and Group#findMembers always sends limit=50, but this same endpoint/model is used by the public discourse/routes/group-members route and templates/group/members.hbs, which have no pagination controls at all (pagination was only added to the admin template). Previously non-automatic groups returned all members and automatic groups up to 200. Now any group with more than 50 members only ever displays the first 50 alphabetically on its public members page.

Members endpoint accepts unbounded and negative limit/offset

limit and offset are taken from params with only to_i and no clamping. A caller who can view a group can pass limit=1000000 to force counting/serializing the entire membership in one request (automatic groups were previously capped at 200), or a negative limit/offset to trigger a database error and a 500. Clamp limit to a sane range (e.g. 1..200) and offset to >= 0.

Group update silently hides the group when the visible parameter is omitted

update guards alias_level with present? and name with an explicit nil check, but assigns group.visible = params[:visible] == "true" unconditionally. Any PUT/PATCH that updates only some fields (for example a rename or alias change from another API client, or the legacy PATCH membership call whose handling was removed) will force visible to false and return success, silently hiding the group. Only assign visible when the parameter is present.

Creating a group discards the alias_level chosen in the form

The admin form always shows the alias_level combo box and Group#asJSON sends alias_level on create, but the new create action only assigns name and visible. A group created with a non-default alias level is saved with the default 0 while the in-memory Ember object still shows the chosen value, so the setting appears applied until the page is reloaded. Assign params[:alias_level] in create as update does.

Stale usernames input leaks between group edit pages

AdminGroupController is a singleton and its new plain `usernames` property is never reset; setupController only sets the model and loads members. Text typed into the Add Members selector for one group is still bound and visible when the admin opens a different group, and clicking Add there would submit the previous group's usernames to the new group. Clear controller usernames (and stale paging state) in setupController or after a successful add.

Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation has a write side effect and counts one signup attempt multiple times

EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves the BlockedEmail row. Validation is not a single commit-time event: UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so one blocked signup attempt increments the counter twice. Any other valid? check, or a save that ultimately fails for an unrelated reason such as the password, also records a match even though no account attempt completed. Separate the pure blocked check from hit recording, or record the hit only once at the point an attempt is actually rejected.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same underlying problem: a query/check method (`should_block_email?` / `should_block?`) has a write side effect of updating match statistics during a read/validation operation. The candidate goes further into the downstream effects during validation, and recommends separating the pure check from hit recording, which directly aligns with the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup can be bypassed by changing email case

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact where(email: email) lookup using the raw user-supplied value, and neither BlockedEmail nor EmailValidator downcases or strips the address before storage or lookup; User.new_from_params also assigns the submitted email unchanged. PostgreSQL string comparison and the unique index are case-sensitive, so an address blocked as bad@spam.example can register as Bad@SPAM.example, and BlockedEmail rows differing only by case can coexist. Normalize the email (for example with Email.downcase and strip) both when creating BlockedEmail records and when checking them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows users to bypass the email block by altering the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write

should_block? loads the BlockedEmail row, does record.match_count += 1 in memory, and saves it. Two concurrent attempts with the same blocked email can both read the same count and both write count+1, losing one hit; the full-row save can also overwrite concurrent changes to the record. Use an atomic database increment such as update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...") or increment_counter instead.

rejectedEmails is shared mutable state on the controller prototype

rejectedEmails is initialized as Em.A([]) in the class definition passed to extend(). In Ember, mutable array/object values declared this way live on the prototype and are shared rather than copied per instance, and createAccount mutates that array with pushObject while nothing ever clears it. Rejected addresses can therefore leak across controller instances and remain rejected for the lifetime of the app/session instead of being scoped to one account-creation flow. Initialize the array per instance (for example in init) and reset it when the create-account modal is shown or closed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items() has incomplete and invalid legacy vendor mappings

flexbox() and inline-flex() emit -moz-box/-moz-inline-box displays, but align-items() provides no -moz-box-align, so alignment is ignored by the legacy Mozilla box implementation for the header centering, .small-action centering, and bullet-badge baseline alignment. The block also emits the non-existent -ms-align-items property at line 121 while the actual IE10 property is -ms-flex-align, so that line is dead code and does not provide the intended support.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: that `-ms-align-items` is a non-existent property and the actual legacy IE property should be `-ms-flex-align`.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mistranslates flex order for legacy WebKit/Mozilla box layout

The order() mixin copies the same value to order and to -webkit-box-ordinal-group/-moz-box-ordinal-group, but the legacy ordinal-group properties are 1-based and unordered items default to group 1, whereas flex order is 0-based and unordered items default to 0. Thus order(0) is invalid for legacy box layout and order(1) collides with unordered items there while following them in modern flex layout; the legacy properties need $val + 1 to preserve the same ordering.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based, whereas standard flex `order` is 0-based, meaning passing 0 (or unadjusted `$val`) causes invalid/incorrect layout in legacy browsers.

Right-floated small-action button loses alignment in new flex container

.small-action is made a flex container at lines 264-265, but its direct-child button still relies on float: right at line 309. Floats do not apply to flex items, and no margin-left: auto, justify-content, or equivalent replacement is added, so the button will sit immediately after .small-action-desc instead of at the right edge of the row.

extra-info-wrapper becomes a flex item without shrink/truncation constraints

Adding order(2) makes .extra-info-wrapper participate as a flex item between the header title and the order(3) panel in the new .d-header .contents flex container, but it gets no flex sizing, min-width: 0, overflow, or truncation rules. A long topic title with category badges therefore cannot shrink below its content size and can push or compress the panel, causing the header controls to overflow or be clipped on narrow widths instead of the topic info truncating.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name include predicate is misnamed and bypasses untrusted-user hiding

The conditional is defined as include_website_name instead of the include_website_name? convention used by ActiveModel Serializers and by the other predicates in this file, so it is never invoked and website_name is always serialized. Additionally, :website_name is absent from untrusted_attributes, which hides :website for TL0 users viewed anonymously. Anonymous visitors therefore receive the host and path derived from a website that was intended to be hidden, and profiles without a website also gain a spurious website_name: nil key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same primary bug: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix (`include_website_name?`) expected by ActiveModel/Rails serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. While their secondary points differ, they directly match on the main issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Same-domain check is asymmetric for apex and www hosts

When the website is http://www.example.com/me and the instance is example.com, the hosts have different label counts, so execution reaches the final branch, which only checks whether the instance host ends with the website host. That check fails and only www.example.com is shown. The reverse configuration, website example.com/me on instance www.example.com, does return example.com/me. The common apex/www combination is therefore handled inconsistently and the requested full path is not shown.

Stripping the first host label falsely matches domains under public suffixes

The sibling-subdomain branch assumes the registrable domain is always the last two labels. For example, website example.co.uk/user and an unrelated instance at other.co.uk both reduce to co.uk after removing the first label, so the serializer incorrectly displays example.co.uk/user as though the website belonged to the instance domain. The same false positive applies to other multi-part public suffixes and shared suffixes such as github.io.

Displayed website text drops query string and fragment

For a matching domain the display text is built from URI#path only. A website such as http://example.com/user?tab=posts#details is displayed as example.com/user even though the actual link points to the full URL, so the supposedly complete URL shown to readers is truncated and can misrepresent the destination, particularly for URLs whose identity is in the query string.

New website_name branches and visibility rules are untested

The added examples cover only an unrelated two-label domain, an exact host match, and a website that is the parent of the instance host. They do not exercise the equal-length sibling-subdomain branch, the apex-versus-www case, a blank or malformed website, or serialization of website_name for a TL0 user viewed anonymously; the untrusted_attributes list in the TL0 context is also unchanged. The untested include predicate and subdomain logic can therefore regress, or leak the hidden website, without any spec failing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Embed URL is interpolated unescaped into raw HTML TopicEmbed.import appends "#{url}" to the post body without HTML-escaping or URL-encoding url. Because the resulting post uses raw_html rendering, a feed- or import-supplied URL containing a single quote can break out of the href attribute and inject additional attributes or markup, for example an onclick handler. The URL must be escaped before it is embedded in the generated footer HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues in TopicEmbed.import: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and an XSS vulnerability from unescaped URL interpolation in generated HTML. The candidate issue directly identifies the exact same XSS vulnerability from unescaped URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without a content field

The job unconditionally calls i.content.scrub. RSS items commonly provide only description/summary rather than content, in which case i.content is nil and this raises NoMethodError. The exception aborts processing of all remaining items, and because the scheduled job is configured with retry: false, a single such item can prevent every later valid feed entry from being imported on each poll.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` may be nil in RSS feeds that only provide `description`, causing a crash (NoMethodError / nil pointer exception).

false_positives.candidate:
Unsanitized feed HTML is stored and rendered as raw HTML

PollFeed passes CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub) directly to TopicEmbed.import without sanitizing it. TopicEmbed.import creates the post with cook_method raw_html, and Post#cook returns raw verbatim for that method, so feed-supplied markup such as script elements or event-handler attributes becomes the post's cooked HTML and is rendered to forum visitors. A malicious or compromised RSS/Atom feed can therefore achieve stored XSS in users' browsers, including administrators.

Embed controller spec expects the old synchronous retriever flow

This spec expects TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve to be called, but EmbedController#best now calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, user_id: ..., embed_url: ...). The mocha expectation will therefore fail, and depending on test job settings the enqueued job may also run for real. The spec should expect Jobs.enqueue with :retrieve_topic and the correct arguments instead.

TopicEmbed.import has a check-then-create race on embed_url

Import first queries TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url) and only creates the embed record if none exists, but concurrent PollFeed and RetrieveTopic jobs (the latter bypasses throttling for staff) can both observe no record for the same new URL and both create a topic/post. The unique database index on embed_url then makes one TopicEmbed.create! raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job and rolling back its work. The creation path needs to handle the uniqueness conflict or serialize creation per URL.

Retrieval throttle key can be left without an expiry

retrieved_recently? sets the Redis throttle key with setnx and only afterwards calls expire as a separate command. If the process crashes or Redis errors between the two commands, the key persists forever with no TTL, permanently blocking retrieval for that embed URL and leaving visitors on the loading page. The key should be created atomically with its 60-second expiry.

Disqus import now depends on the original site being reachable

The import previously created the topic locally from the Disqus export, but now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...), which fetches t[:link] over HTTP. If a thread's link is missing, malformed, or the original article is offline, open() raises or TopicEmbed.import returns nil and that thread's Disqus comments are skipped or the whole import aborts, losing data that is fully present in the export file. The removed --category option also means existing import invocations using it will fail and imported topics can no longer be placed in a category.

absolutize_urls mishandles common relative URL forms

Only href/src values beginning with '/' are rewritten. Plain relative references such as images/photo.jpg are left relative and will resolve against the Discourse host, producing broken links/images, while protocol-relative references such as //cdn.example.com/photo.jpg are incorrectly rewritten onto the source origin as http://source.example.com//cdn.example.com/photo.jpg. URL resolution should use URI joining against the source URL instead of string prefix checks.

Unauthenticated clients can flood retrieval with non-canonical URLs

Recurring cancellation duplicates deletes with wrong credentials

The new outer loop iterates every calendar reference, and inside the recurring/allRemainingBookings branch it again maps over all of the organizer's calendar credentials and, for each updated booking, picks only the first calendar reference via find(). Each recurring event is therefore delete-attempted once per reference times per credential, mostly with a credential that does not own that reference's uid/externalCalendarId. This produces spurious delete failures (and possible wrong-calendar deletions) for collective recurring bookings instead of deleting each reference once with its own credentialId.

Confirming a collective booking only creates the organizer's calendar event

The evt built for handleConfirmation contains only booking.destinationCalendar or the confirming user's destinationCalendar as a single-element array, with no destination calendars for the other collective hosts. Since EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents now creates events solely by iterating evt.destinationCalendar, a requires-confirmation collective booking that is later confirmed will only create an event for one host, defeating the multi-host fix on the confirmation path. The Stripe/PayPal webhook handlers build the same single-destination evt.

Collective team calendars are dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and the collective merge then does evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars). With null, the optional chain silently no-ops, so all collected team hosts' destination calendars are lost and EventManager falls back to the first connected calendar instead of creating an event per host.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach leaves calendar/video deletion fire-and-forget

The forEach callback was made async to await getCalendar, but Array.prototype.forEach ignores the returned promises. Reschedule therefore proceeds to send the reschedule email and return true without waiting for calendar.deleteEvent or deleteMeeting to even start (the await on getCalendar defers them past the forEach), so in a request-scoped/serverless execution the old events can be left behind, and any rejection becomes an unhandled rejection that the surrounding try/catch cannot catch. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` or a for...of loop.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: using `forEach` with an `async` callback for calendar/video deletions, resulting in unawaited promises ('fire-and-forget'), unhandled rejections, and incomplete cleanup, and suggests the same fixes (`Promise.all` with `map` or `for...of`).

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are started eagerly for every app

Every value in the appStore object literal is an import() call, so all 28 calls are evaluated as soon as this module is loaded. Code that needs only one app (for example getCalendar for a single credential) therefore still starts loading every calendar, video, CRM, and payment app and retains all of their side effects and memory/startup cost, defeating the intended per-app lazy loading. A rejected import for an app that is never used can also surface later as an unhandled rejection from the cached promise. Store thunks such as `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and invoke the thunk at lookup time instead.

requestReschedule does not wait for old calendar/video deletion

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach now takes an async callback whose promise is discarded. Immediately afterwards the mutation sends the reschedule email and webhooks and returns, while the awaited getCalendar/deleteEvent and deleteMeeting work is still pending; it may be abandoned when the request ends and its failures are unhandled, leaving the supposedly cancelled calendar event and video meeting active. Await the deletions with Promise.all over map (or a for...of loop) before continuing.

Recurring-cancellation deletions can miss the later Promise.all entirely

For recurring bookings, calendar deletions are collected by pushing into apiDeletes from inside an async forEach callback that first awaits getCalendar and then awaits deleteEvent before pushing. The handler later awaits Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)), but concat snapshots apiDeletes at that moment, typically before those async callbacks have pushed anything. The handler can therefore delete the booking's attendees/references (losing the external uids needed to retry) and return while the external calendar deletions are not awaited or have not run, orphaning events on users' calendars. Collect the deletion promises synchronously via map/Promise.all or a sequential for...of and await them before the database cleanup completes.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes accepts zero and negative values

The new --flusher-processes option accepts any integer. In SpanFlusher, 0 is treated as unset because it uses `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so `--flusher-processes 0` unexpectedly starts one heavy spawned Sentry/Kafka-producer process per assigned shard. Negative values flow into `min()` and shard modulo indexing, which can raise a KeyError or start no flusher workers during consumer construction. Validate this as a positive integer, for example with click.IntRange(min=1) and equivalent validation in SpanFlusher/ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.

Comma-joined shard list corrupts metrics tags

When one flusher process handles multiple shards, which is the normal case when flusher_processes is smaller than the shard count and always the case for the CLI default of 1, `shard_tag` becomes a value such as `0,1,2`. Passing that comma-containing value as a StatsD/DogStatsD tag makes the backend parse it as `shard:0` plus stray tags `1` and `2`, so the produce, wait-produce, and segment-size metrics cannot be correctly attributed by shard. Emit these metrics per flushed segment/shard or otherwise use a single sanitized shard tag value.

Multi-shard flusher test never flushes any spans

test_flusher_processes_limit creates four shards mapped to two flusher processes, but it only asserts process counts and then joins without submitting spans or advancing the flush clock. The existing basic test covers only one shard/process, so the central new behavior—a shared process correctly flushing, producing, and completing segments for multiple shards, without drops or duplicates—is untested. Add an end-to-end test that stores spans across several shards with fewer flusher processes than shards and asserts the produced segments for each shard.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
PR-comment helpers are defined on the integration class but invoked on the workflow class

The new _truncate_title, get_environment_info, and get_merged_pr_single_issue_template helpers are added to CommitContextIntegration, but GitHubPRCommentWorkflow and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow call self.get_environment_info() and self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(); those workflows inherit from PRCommentWorkflow/OpenPRCommentWorkflow, not CommitContextIntegration. Generating the first suspect-issue comment will therefore raise AttributeError and fail the PR/MR comment workflow instead of posting the comment. The helpers should live on PRCommentWorkflow (or be called via self.integration) and the truncation call should reference the class that actually defines it.

Error timestamps and replay-segment timestamps are compared in different units

fetch_error_details stores the error event timestamp from nodestore, which is epoch seconds, while replay recording-segment (rrweb) events carry epoch milliseconds. gen_request_data then directly compares error_events[i]['timestamp'] < event.get('timestamp'), so with real data an error timestamp in seconds will almost always be smaller than a segment timestamp in milliseconds and all errors will be emitted before the first breadcrumb (or in the wrong position), destroying the chronological context sent to Seer. Normalize both sides to the same unit (for example multiply the error timestamp by 1000) before sorting/comparing; the added tests mask this by using seconds for the segment timestamps as well.

Hidden span attributes are only hidden while a search query is active

sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns the full sorted attribute list unchanged when the search box is empty, and only applies the HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES exclusion (is_segment, project_id, received) inside the branch that runs when a search query is present. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

Group authorization resources are created with the group ID as the resource name, while Resource.getId() is an unrelated internal authorization-store UUID. This loop calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...), which does findByName(server, UUID) and therefore misses the per-group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource, and then adds that same UUID to the granted set. Callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser and getUsersCount expect actual GroupModel IDs in UserModel.GROUPS, so per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS grants are not correctly used to filter or count group members. This Account UI resource uses i18next-style double-brace placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, etc.) throughout the file, but error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed to Java MessageFormat syntax: {0}, {1}, and {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}. i18next does not evaluate MessageFormat choice expressions, so this value will render literal or unresolved placeholders instead of the interpolated limits and pluralized noun. Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 was replaced with Italian text

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong substring and inverts the comparison

For a normal ID such as onrtac the checked substring is 'ta', never 'ac', so expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken pass regardless of the encoded grant type as long as the raw part is a UUID; the new grant-encoding behaviour is effectively untested by these integration assertions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcut length is documented inconsistently and never validated

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() javadoc describes the value as 'usually like 3-letters', but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider encodes session, token and grant shortcuts without validating length and getTokenContextFromTokenId() requires the whole encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters, i.e. exactly 2 characters per shortcut. A factory following the javadoc and returning a 3-letter shortcut, or returning a 1-letter/empty/null shortcut, produces token IDs that the decoder rejects, or fails with an NPE from the ConcurrentHashMap, instead of being rejected clearly at startup. Document exactly two characters and validate uniqueness and length in postInit() and in the lazy refresh paths.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same documentation mismatch: getShortcut() suggests three-letter shortcuts while actual usage expects two-letter shortcuts. Its additional validation concerns and stronger recommendation do not negate this overlap.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks custom grant-type factories

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an extension interface, but getShortcut() was added as an abstract method without a default implementation. Existing custom grant factories compiled against the old interface will fail with AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates all OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut(), and source implementations will no longer compile. This can break server startup or token issuance for deployments with custom grants. Provide a default implementation, for example returning the unknown shortcut, so existing factories continue to work.

Public OAuth2GrantType.Context copy constructor was removed

The previously public Context(Context) copy constructor has been removed while changing the main constructor to derive grantType from formParams. Code in custom grant types or delegating/wrapping grant implementations that used new OAuth2GrantType.Context(existingContext) will now fail to compile, and already-compiled code will fail with NoSuchMethodError. The copy constructor should be retained, copying grantType as well, or at least deprecated through a compatibility cycle.

Unknown grant type now fails all access-token issuance instead of falling back

TokenManager.initToken() calls encodeTokenId() for every access token, and encodeTokenId() throws IllegalStateException when the GRANT_TYPE client-session attribute is a non-null value that is not exactly a registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory id. Token creation previously succeeded in that situation, and getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext() already treats a missing grant as the unknown value 'na'; an unregistered, aliased, or extension-supplied grant string now turns token issuance into a server error instead of using the same unknown fallback.

Decoding throws on malformed or newer token IDs instead of returning UNKNOWN

getTokenContextFromTokenId() returns UNKNOWN for legacy token IDs without a colon, but throws IllegalArgumentException for any colon-containing ID whose prefix is not exactly 6 characters or whose session/token/grant shortcut is unknown to this node. That is inconsistent backward-compatibility handling: during rolling upgrades, or when the planned introspection/userinfo consumers decode tokens issued by a newer node with a new shortcut, validation would fail with an exception rather than falling back to the normal session lookup. Unknown or malformed encodings should be treated like legacy IDs and return UNKNOWN context.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login form crashes when federated credential cannot be retrieved

The bean calls credentialModelOpt.get() without checking whether RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) found a credential, and line 21 also calls getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() without checking for an exhausted credential. For federated users, configuredFor/isConfiguredFor and getFederatedCredentialsStream are independent storage-provider operations: a provider can report the user as configured and validate codes while returning no credential model, or can return a credential whose codes are all used. In either case rendering the recovery-code login form throws NoSuchElementException instead of showing the form, potentially locking the user out.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked Optional.get() call on the credential returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user), which can throw NoSuchElementException when empty. Its additional discussion of exhausted codes does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Successful federated recovery code is not consumed

After credentialManager.isValid succeeds, this code only deletes the credential if the retrieved model already reports allCodesUsed(); it never persists a used state for the code that was just consumed. The storage implementation added by this PR likewise validates by checking whether any stored raw code equals the input and does not remove or mark that code, while its getCredentials method recreates every stored code as unused. Therefore, with the PR's federated implementation, the same recovery code can be replayed indefinitely, the prompt continues to request the first code, and the all-used regeneration path is never reached, defeating the single-use property of recovery codes.

Creating codes in user storage leaves an existing local credential valid

When updateCredential succeeds in user storage, the method only logs and does not remove or disable any recovery-code credential already stored in Keycloak's local database. This matters on upgrade and regeneration: before this change, recovery codes for federated users were always created locally, so regenerating them after the change creates a different set in user storage while the old local set remains. Credential validation can still accept credentials from either store even though getCredential prefers the federated set for display, so rotating recovery codes does not reliably invalidate the previous, possibly compromised, codes.

No test for federated user falling back to local storage or for code consumption

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin covers only the branch where the test storage accepts the recovery credential and then logs in once using the first code. It does not cover a federated user whose storage rejects updateCredential and therefore must receive and use a local credential, nor does it verify that a used code cannot be reused, that the next requested code advances, that exhausted codes trigger regeneration, or that regenerated codes invalidate the old set. Those are the main new branches and security semantics introduced by the change, so regressions in them would not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Default-strategy deployments are created without the required rolling-updates feature

createInitialDeployment() returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, before enabling Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES. true_positives.matched_candidate:

Any existing out-of-tree or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration calls CryptoProvider::order during provider detection, and source implementations or mocks will no longer compile. Providers are now sorted only by order(), while DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200. If more than one of them is accidentally present, the previous explicit 'multiple crypto providers' error is replaced by silently choosing whichever ServiceLoader/classpath ordering returns first. This can silently select the non-FIPS provider in a deployment expecting FIPS, and ServiceLoader instantiation can already have run the other providers' constructors and their global Java Security provider registration side effects. Built-in providers need distinct priorities or ties at the highest order should remain an error.

ES384 and ES512 tests reuse a default-curve key and only assert round-trip identity

The test creates one EC key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so it does not create P-384 or P-521 keys for ES384/ES512. It then only asserts that concatenated R/S converted to DER and back equals the padded concatenated value, without verifying the DER signature against the public key, comparing it with the original JCA DER signature, or checking the expected curve-specific lengths. Defects in 48/66-byte R/S handling, leading-zero stripping, or the long-form DER length needed for real ES512 signatures can therefore pass undetected. Each algorithm should generate a key on its corresponding curve and verify the reconverted DER signature.

Malformed zero-length ASN.1 integer escapes as NumberFormatException instead of IOException

readInteger() passes the decoded byte array directly to new BigInteger(bytes). A malformed DER integer with length 0 makes that constructor throw NumberFormatException, although callers such as asn1derToConcatenatedRS() are written to handle IOException for invalid signatures. Invalid input can consequently abort processing with an unchecked exception instead of the declared, handled error type. Zero-length and otherwise invalid integer encodings should be rejected with IOException before constructing the BigInteger.

The factory creates FixedQueuePool once during construction, while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts that pool down. Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory when partitions are revoked and reassigned, so the new strategy receives workers that have exited and queues on which shutdown() has already been called. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that exception and marks the offset complete, allowing messages to be committed without being processed. A normal Kafka rebalance can therefore cause silent data loss until the process is restarted.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run() logs an exception from result_processor but unconditionally calls complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop can consequently commit the offset for a result that was never successfully handled, contradicting the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing and causing failed uptime results to be lost rather than redelivered.

Unbounded queues provide no Arroyo backpressure

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and therefore has no maximum size, and submit() never raises MessageRejected or otherwise blocks. If workers process more slowly than Kafka delivers, Arroyo can continue submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory use and hiding the backlog from Kafka flow control. This also makes the class documentation's claim of natural backpressure when queues fill up incorrect because these queues never fill.

Close stops offset committing before workers finish and shutdown drops queued work

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() stops and joins the commit thread before shutting down the queue pool, so results completed by workers afterward have no commit loop left to commit their offsets and will be redelivered. In addition, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False); a busy worker exits after its current item instead of draining its queue. Graceful close therefore both leaves processed offsets uncommitted and abandons queued work rather than finishing it within the strategy's join period.

Python's salted hash does not provide consistent group-to-queue assignment

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() for a string group key. Python randomizes string hashing per interpreter unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed, so the same subscription can map to different queues after a restart or when processed by another consumer process. That undermines the documented consistent-assignment and per-group ordering guarantee across rebalances and deployments; a stable digest such as hashlib.md5 or sha256 should be used instead.

Invalid max_workers values are silently accepted for thread-queue-parallel mode

The CLI accepts any integer for --max-workers, and this code converts 0 to 20 with 'or' while passing a negative value through as num_queues. A negative value creates no queues or workers; submissions then fail with an index/modulo error, are caught by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), and are marked complete, so their offsets can be committed without processing. The option should be validated as a positive integer before constructing the pool.

Blocked offsets make commit checks repeatedly scan an ever-growing set

OffsetTracker retains every offset after a blocked or very slow offset, because offsets can only be removed after a contiguous commit. get_committable_offsets() is called once per second and computes both min() and max() over that retained set each time. During exactly the slow-item backlog this feature is meant to tolerate, the set can grow to a large number of completed offsets and the commit loop becomes repeated O(n) work while also retaining unbounded tracking state.

Negative cursor offsets are passed to Django queryset slicing, which does not support them

The optimized branch deliberately uses cursor.offset as the slice start when enable_advanced_features is set, and BasePaginator at line 182 likewise preserves negative offsets for is_prev cursors. The claim that Django ORM handles this is false: Django QuerySet slicing asserts 'Negative indexing is not supported', so a crafted cursor such as a negative-offset prev/next cursor produces a 500 rather than safely paging from the end. true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime ordering of its only caller

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key), and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer. Its only caller orders AuditLogEntry by -datetime, for which DateTimePaginator is required: it converts epoch-millis cursor values to timezone-aware datetimes and formats item keys with strftime. With -datetime, build_queryset receives an integer instead of a datetime and build_cursor calls math.floor on a datetime, so the optimized audit-log path will raise TypeError/database comparison errors instead of returning a page.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies math.floor/math.ceil being applied to a datetime key in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key when ordering by '-datetime', causing TypeError—the same underlying bug as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Unrelated audit-log change enables unvetted advanced pagination for non-superusers

This spans-buffer PR also switches the audit-log endpoint to OptimizedCursorPaginator when optimized_pagination=true is supplied and the caller is a superuser OR merely has organization_context.member.has_global_access. has_global_access is team-access scope for ordinary organization members, not proof of administrator/superuser status as the comment claims. This exposes a separate, user-controlled pagination implementation on a sensitive endpoint, unrelated to span buffering, and should be removed or reviewed/tested as its own API change.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts span end-timestamp scores on overlaps

The old SUNIONSTORE deduplicated identical payloads without changing metadata. The new redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key) uses Redis' default AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both sorted sets (duplicate delivery, a merge of overlapping partial segments, or destination/source overlap) gets score roughly end_timestamp+end_timestamp instead of its end timestamp. That corrupts the score later used by zpopmin eviction, artificially protecting duplicated spans and causing other spans to be evicted first. Use an explicit AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve one real timestamp.

SET-to-ZSET switch breaks in-flight Redis segments with WRONGTYPE errors

Existing buffered segment keys were created as Redis SETs by sadd and can remain live until the one-hour redis_ttl/flush timeouts expire. This change immediately issues ZADD in process_spans, and the Lua script likewise issues ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN, while flush uses ZSCAN. Redis returns WRONGTYPE when a sorted-set command is used on an existing SET key, so during rollout process_spans fails for traces already buffered, batches retry/stall, and unflushed spans can be lost when the old keys expire. The PR contains no key versioning, drain, dual-type handling, or other migration for in-flight keys.

Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed while insert cap ignores the configured limit

_load_segment_data no longer enforces SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans; after this change that constructor setting is effectively dead. Eviction is instead hardcoded to 1000 in add-buffer.lua, so the default changes from 1001 to 1000 and any custom max_segment_spans value is silently ignored. Segments that bypass insert eviction, including pre-existing large segments, are now loaded and emitted regardless of span count, bounded only by max_segment_bytes, increasing memory and downstream segment-size risk.

Redirect resolution depth silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop previously allowed 10000 hops, with a comment acknowledging that deeper segment trees might not be joined correctly. Reducing it to 1000 makes that failure mode ten times more likely: when the cap is exhausted the script proceeds with an unresolved set_span_id and no error, so spans for a deep chain can be placed in a different segment key and flushed as split/incomplete segments rather than being joined to their root segment.

Insert-time eviction silently drops spans with no metric or truncation signal

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin permanently discards the earliest-ending spans during insert. Unlike the removed flush-time span-count guard, which emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded and logged the segment size, this path emits no metric/log and marks the flushed segment in no way as truncated. Operators cannot measure span loss and downstream consumers receive an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one.

No test covers the new eviction, sorted-set merge, or score behavior

The test changes only add the newly required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment, asserts which spans zpopmin retains, covers duplicate payloads across merged partial segments, or verifies that scores remain real end timestamps after ZUNIONSTORE. The central data-loss behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset instead of the dataset actually being queried

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which is the dataset that will execute the query, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable dataset from the request. The dashboard-split factory calls _get_event_stats with different datasets, including discover for error splits and the scoped dataset for transaction-like splits. Consequently, an error split can incorrectly miss upsampling, while a metrics or transaction-like query can receive upsampled_count() even though that builder or table does not support sample_weight. The decision should be based on scoped_dataset and the query actually being executed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer request dataset instead of scoped_dataset, causing discover queries such as dashboard error splits to incorrectly skip upsampling. The candidate adds a potential consequence but clearly matches the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Error-focus detection ignores the actual query and uses a naive substring check

The transform decision reads only request.GET['query'] and checks whether it contains 'event.type:error'. _get_event_stats is not given the opportunity to pass its query argument, which may be an internally constructed dashboard query such as '(...) AND !event.type:transaction' or a widget query that differs from the request parameter. The substring check also misses forms such as '!event.type:transaction' and 'event.type:[error, default]', while incorrectly matching the negated query '!event.type:error'. Error charts can therefore remain unupsampled, or non-error queries can have count() replaced by a sum of sample_weight.

upsampled_count has no fallback for missing sample weights and truncates fractional weights

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested before error sampling was enabled, or that otherwise have a null or zero sample_weight, contribute nothing instead of counting as one event, so historical and unsampled errors disappear from upsampled series. Additionally, toInt64 truncates fractional sums produced by float sample weights, systematically undercounting estimated errors. Missing weights should default to 1 and the fractional estimate should be rounded or retained rather than truncated.

Internal upsampled_count function is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike neighboring internal-only aggregation helpers. It therefore expands the public Discover function surface and can be requested directly through query builders using DiscoverDatasetConfig, bypassing the stats endpoint's project-allowlist and dataset checks. On non-allowlisted projects or datasets backed by tables without meaningful error sample weights, this can return misleading counts or produce invalid Snuba queries. The function should remain internal to the gated transformation.

Cached allowlist eligibility can remain stale and the invalidation helper is never used

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds, but invalidate_upsampling_cache has no caller in this change and there is no hook from option changes to that helper. After a project is removed from issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist, the endpoint can continue replacing count() with upsampled counts; after a project is added, it can continue returning raw counts until the entry expires. Either wire invalidation to allowlist changes or remove the unused invalidation API and explicitly accept only TTL-based expiry.

Stray subproject file is unrelated to the feature

This change adds a root-level 'sentry-repo' file containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a'. That resembles an accidentally recorded nested-repository gitlink without any corresponding submodule configuration and is unrelated to error upsampling. It can confuse checkout and submodule tooling and should be removed before merging.

Tests do not exercise the public eligibility entry point used by the endpoint

The unit tests import and test only the private helpers _are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, and the column transform. They do not test is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, the only function called by organization_events_stats, including its caching behavior, dataset handling, or interaction with a scoped/split dataset. The Snuba tests also cover only events that already carry client_sample_rate=0.1, leaving unsampled events and the resulting sample_weight behavior unverified, so regressions in the actual production path can pass the added tests.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored

The test named "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}; despite the comment saying this allows access, checkPermission treats a false map value as no permission, and the fake permission store also returns no granting permission. The request therefore denies through the ordinary cached/DB path even if permDenialCache is never consulted, so the test does not prove the new short-circuit works. It should configure the underlying store or permission cache to allow dash1, or assert that the permission store is not called when the denial entry is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous

userPermDenialCacheKey joins variable-length UID, action, name, and parent values with plain underscores and no escaping, length prefixes, or hashing. Distinct tuples can consequently produce the same key: for example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. Grafana resource and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny a different resource until the entry expires. Build the key from a structured, unambiguously encoded or hashed tuple.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey, which can cause distinct component tuples to collide and produce incorrect denial cache hits affecting permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include the identity type

The denial key is built only from namespace, the raw subject UID, action, resource name, and parent folder, but permission resolution switches on identity type and returns different permission sets for the same UID. In particular, anonymous and render-service subjects both use UID "0", while anonymous receives Viewer-role permissions and the render service is granted read access to all dashboards and folders. A denial recorded for anonymous:0 can therefore short-circuit and incorrectly deny render:0 for the same dashboard for up to the denial TTL, and the same collision can occur between user and service-account spellings. The key must include the identity type, preferably together with the canonical resolved UID.

Denial entries shadow fresher permissions and undermine immediate access after a grant

Check consults permDenialCache before checking the ordinary permission cache, and neither getUserPermissions' permission-cache refresh nor List's refresh deletes existing denial entries. After a permission is granted, such as the creator permission inserted for a new dashboard or folder, a later check or list for another resource can refresh permCache with a scope map that now allows the denied resource, yet checks for that resource will still return the old denial until the denial TTL expires. A denial recorded by a check made just before the grant has the same effect. This partially defeats the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created resources immediately; cached allowances should be honoured before denials or denials should be invalidated when permissions are refreshed.

Every distinct cached denial now forces a database permission fetch

When cached permissions do not allow a check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the permission-store cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so this performs a fresh database permission query. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent tuple for 30 seconds. A user checking many distinct dashboards or folders they do not own therefore causes one permission query per resource instead of one query per user/action as before, multiplying database load in denial-heavy or enumeration-heavy workloads and increasing cache cardinality. The revalidation needs a freshness or negative-cache strategy that does not scale database queries with the number of distinct denied resources.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The JPA-backed getForLogin result, however, is based on the stored enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC fields and does not exclude IdPs merely because their organization is disabled. Therefore, for an IdP in a disabled organization that currently qualifies in the stored data, changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly to a disqualifying value makes both the wrapped original and the updated model fail getLoginPredicate(), so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() returns without invalidating any login cache. The cache therefore conflates the two cases, so getForLogin(ORG_ONLY or ALL, "") can return the cached all-organizations result, or the reverse ordering can make a null-organization request reuse an empty/specific-organization result.
