true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs without justification

This changes the interval for CleanUpService.Run from 10 minutes to 1 minute. That ticker drives every job in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp-user invites, short URLs, and query-history enforcement will now run 10x as often, increasing database and log load in every Grafana instance. The PR description only justifies splitting the annotation DELETE statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks and does not mention or justify this frequency change, so it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or separately justified and scoped to annotations.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load from more frequent cleanup execution. The candidate adds detail and recommendations but addresses the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Parameter-limit workaround only handles SQLite, regressing large batches on other databases

deleteByIDs binds one '?' placeholder per fetched ID for every database except the special-cased SQLite path at lines 608-613. The previous implementation used a subquery DELETE with no per-ID bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable and this PR's own test raises it to 32767; a larger configured batch (over 65535 parameters) will now fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL with bind-parameter limits even though the old statement would have succeeded, aborting cleanup partway. The workaround should be based on len(ids) and the actual database's parameter limit, or IDs should be chunked/inlined for all affected dialects.

SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

For SQLite with batch size over 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of up to batch-size IDs (32767 in the added test, applied repeatedly to annotations and orphaned tags) is O(n^2) in time and allocations and can make large cleanups and the new test very slow. Use strings.Builder (or chunk the deletes) instead of re-formatting the whole string per ID.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts legacy-versus-storage latency and error measurements and, for Delete, creates a high-cardinality kind label containing user object names.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies successful Delete passing the object name instead of options.Kind as the metrics kind label, matching the golden issue. The additional metric attribution concerns do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object

Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result

Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. Mode 3 performs legacy writes asynchronously with no completion signal, so those assertions race the background legacy write and can intermittently observe missing or stale legacy playlists even when the implementation eventually succeeds. The mode 3 scenarios need eventual-consistency polling for legacy assertions or a different set of expectations from the synchronous modes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key

The switch previously rendered GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}; the replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits the key while the datasource and unknown branches keep theirs. In this dynamically appended/filtered list, index-based reconciliation can reuse the wrong component instance and its local state such as modals, drawers, and menus, in addition to producing React key warnings. Restore key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem and the resulting reconciliation/rendering issues when the list changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence action opens no drawer for Prometheus-only rules

In the new list view RuleActionsButtons receives only promRule, so `rule` is undefined. Clicking Silence in AlertRuleMenu sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but this line only mounts SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. The click therefore has no visible effect and silencing from the alert list is broken, even though the new prom abilities may show the Silence menu item.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same mismatch: list views pass only promRule, while the silence drawer requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Consequently, the enabled Silence menu action toggles state but never renders the drawer, producing no visible effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Pause action is never rendered for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

The new list view supplies only a promRule and no rulerRule, and this PR computes canPause from the new Grafana prom abilities. Rendering still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule), which is false when rulerRule is undefined, and MenuItemPauseRule also requires that ruler rule. Consequently Pause never appears in the new rule list even for editable, unpaused Grafana rules, despite the newly added ability check.

Delete action is never rendered for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

canDelete can now become true through useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when only a promRule is available, but the Delete menu item is additionally gated by `rulerRule &&` and its handler is typed to require a RulerRuleDTO. In the new GrafanaGroupLoader/FilterView list, rulerRule is always undefined, so users with delete permission cannot delete a rule from the list. The GrafanaGroupLoader test even encodes this by expecting only four menu items despite granting delete permission.

skipToken does not actually skip Grafana prom abilities

Callers pass skipToken for cloud rules, non-Grafana prom rules, or absent prom rules, but useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts it to undefined and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities still computes real abilities. For an undefined rule, Duplicate becomes [AlwaysSupported, Grafana-rule-create permission] because provisioned/plugin checks are false and loading is false. AlertRuleMenu ORs this with the ruler result, so Duplicate can appear for cloud or ruler-only rules based solely on an unrelated Grafana create permission. A skipped rule should return [false, false] for every action.

Federated rule groups lose their immutable status

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) for CombinedRules and marked federated rules unsupported for Update/Delete. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which discards the group and hardcodes isFederated to false. Federated Mimir rule groups in existing CombinedRule consumers will therefore be offered edit/delete actions that federated groups do not support.

Grafana recording rules can no longer be paused

The ruler-based ability used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules, for Pause/Restore. The new prom-based ability uses isAlertingRule instead, so Pause and Restore are unsupported for Grafana recording rules. Since the list view no longer supplies a ruler rule to provide the old ability, recording rules lose pause/unpause entirely.

Shard-split queries are interpolated multiple times

runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target here, but splitQueriesByStreamShard (line 163) then passes those targets to runSplitQuery, which at querySplitting.ts:299 calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables again for every shard/time sub-request; the updated shard test even expects 5 applyTemplateVariables calls for one original query. Loki's applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters adhoc filters into the stream selector and re-runs template replacement, neither of which is guaranteed idempotent: repeated passes can add the same adhoc matcher again and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by a first-pass variable value, besides re-parsing already-interpolated LogQL per chunk. Interpolation should be owned by one layer, e.g. the shard layer should be able to tell runSplitQuery its targets are already interpolated.

Split queries are interpolated again by datasource.runQuery for every chunk

The queries interpolated here are built into grouped sub-requests and executed via datasource.runQuery in runSplitGroupedQueries (line 180). Loki's runQuery backend path (DataSourceWithBackend.query) applies applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and request.filters before sending each chunk to the backend, so every split query is now interpolated at least twice, and three times on the shard path. As with the shard double-interpolation, the repeated adhoc-filter injection from request.filters and repeated templateSrv replacement of already-substituted values are not guaranteed idempotent and can corrupt or invalidly duplicate stream-selector matchers. The early interpolation for splitting decisions needs to be reconciled with the downstream one, rather than simply adding another pass.

Queries that interpolate to empty are no longer filtered out before sharding

The order was changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate: lines 49-52 test the pre-interpolation expr, so a target such as '$SELECTOR' that resolves to an empty string was previously dropped but now survives into groupTargetsByQueryType, requestSupportsSharding/getSelectorForShardValues and fetchLabelValues with an empty stream selector. It is only dropped later by runSplitQuery's own pre-interpolation filter, which can leave that call with no grouped requests instead of the query simply being ignored as an empty query. Add a post-interpolation expr filter (and apply the same filter-after-interpolate ordering in runSplitQuery).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one database session and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction, lock, or database constraint enforcing the maximum row count. Two concurrent requests for different new devices, on the same or different Grafana instances, can both observe count == deviceLimit-1 and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. The per-process local cache does not coordinate distinct device IDs or multiple instances. The count check and admission of a new device need to be made atomic, for example with a locking transaction or another database-enforced mechanism.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend transactions or locking to make admission atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected devices are cached and then allowed on the next request

tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache with SetDefault before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and it never evicts that entry when the store returns an error. A new device over the limit therefore fails once with ErrDeviceLimitReached, but its next request on the same instance within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early cache return, TagDevice reports success, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity even though the device was never inserted. Concurrent requests can also observe the cache entry set by an in-flight request that is later rejected. Set the cache only after a successful store write, or delete the entry on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds and leaves it cached after ErrDeviceLimitReached, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit during the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider signature changes are not reflected in dependency wiring

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changes its third parameter from anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore in anonstore/database.go additionally changes from accepting only db.DB to requiring an int64 deviceLimit. The checked-in Wire injector/provider wiring that calls these constructors is not updated or regenerated in this PR, so code generated/called with the old arguments no longer compiles and Wire has no ordinary injectable int64 binding for the new store parameter. Update and regenerate the wiring, or keep the store injectable and supply the configured limit through its existing provider wiring.

Anonymous authentication now blocks on device tagging without a timeout

Authenticate previously tagged devices in a goroutine with panic recovery and a two-minute background-context timeout. It now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context and no timeout or recovery. A slow or blocked anon_device count/insert therefore stalls anonymous authentication for the full database/request duration, request cancellation can abort the limit decision, and a panic in tagging now propagates into request authentication instead of merely degrading tagging. Use a bounded context for the now-synchronous enforcement call and preserve appropriate panic handling.

New device_limit setting is absent from shipped configuration definitions

The PR parses auth.anonymous/device_limit into Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit, but it does not add device_limit to conf/defaults.ini, the sample configuration, or the Grafana configuration documentation. Operators therefore cannot discover the new limit from the shipped configuration, and configuration/environment handling that enumerates known keys may not surface it consistently. Add the default and explanatory documentation alongside the existing auth.anonymous settings.

Device-limit tests do not cover allowed updates or the service authentication path

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second distinct device is rejected by the store when the limit is 1. It does not verify the intended complementary behavior that the already-admitted device can still be updated while count >= limit, and no test exercises AnonDeviceService.TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate repeatedly after a rejection. Those missing cases leave both the updateDevice success path and service-level enforcement behaviour unverified. Add tests for updating the existing device at the limit and for repeated service-level requests from a rejected device.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded on the translation path

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale), while ApplicationController#set_locale is the only caller of I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Code outside a web request, such as background jobs and mailers, and translations using an explicit locale: option can therefore invoke the new Fallbacks backend before the site-default and :en YAML files have been lazily loaded. Those lookups return 'translation missing' instead of falling back; for calls without interpolation arguments, that missing string is also stored frozen in the LRU cache keyed only by key and locale, so it can continue to be served after a later request loads :en until cache eviction or reload. All fallback locales for the effective or explicit locale should be loaded inside translate/lookup before consulting or caching the backend.

Custom fallbacks object discards I18n::Locale::Fallbacks behavior

FallbackLocaleList inherits directly from Hash and replaces the I18n::Locale::Fallbacks object previously configured by Rails, but its [] ignores anything stored in the hash and the class provides neither Locale::Fallbacks' defaults nor its map configuration API. It also loses parent-tag expansion: for a locale such as en_GB, a missing key is resolved in SiteSetting.default_locale before its parent :en, because :en appears only as the final entry. Existing or plugin code using the documented fallbacks API can therefore be silently ignored or fail, and regional locales can receive the site language instead of their parent language. The custom ordering should be implemented by subclassing or extending I18n::Locale::Fallbacks rather than replacing it with a plain Hash.

Every backend lookup now consults SiteSetting

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] for every uncached translation, localization, and pluralization lookup, and this implementation calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every such call. That puts the DB-backed settings subsystem on the hot translation path that translate_accelerator otherwise optimizes through lazy loading and caching, and it also makes translations attempted during boot, rake, or asset tasks depend on SiteSetting being loadable before the fallback chain can even be computed. The chain should be cached and invalidated when default_locale changes, rather than recomputed through SiteSetting for each lookup.

No tests cover the custom fallback backend or lazy loading

This change replaces the Rails fallback configuration with a custom Hash, moves pluralization setup into config/initializers/i18n.rb, removes config.i18n.fallbacks from the environment files, and adds lazy loading of fallback locales, but it adds no specs. Nothing verifies that a key missing from the user locale falls back first to the site default and then to :en, that the relevant locale files are loaded outside ApplicationController, or that pluralized strings obtained through a fallback still use the fallback locale's pluralization rules. Regressions would surface only as wrong-language text or 'translation missing' strings in production.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil requests panic before LoggerMiddleware's nil guards can run

QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics dereference req.PluginContext without a nil check. LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards nil requests and passes them through (logger_middleware.go:63, 77, 90, 104), but in CreateMiddlewares the contextual middleware sits in front of it (pluginsintegration.go:160-161), so a nil request now panics in this middleware instead of reaching the guarded pass-through/downstream error handling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same nil-request panic in ContextualLoggerMiddleware's QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics methods caused by accessing req.PluginContext without a nil check. It also describes the regression from bypassing the existing middleware's nil guards.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the receiver's recorded logs

FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of returning the receiver or a logger sharing its state. LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx) (logger_middleware.go:58), so a test holding the original TestLogger and asserting on InfoLogs will observe zero calls even though a log was emitted; the fake therefore no longer behaves like the real logger (which writes to the same underlying output) and will silently hide the new Plugin Request Completed log in tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that TestLogger.FromContext returns a new logger instead of the receiver, causing logs to be recorded on a separate instance and assertions against the original logger to miss them.

false_positives.candidate:
Streaming endpoints do not receive the contextual logger

SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the original context to next without calling instrumentContext, unlike QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics. These request types also carry a PluginContext, so any logging performed downstream via a contextual logger during streaming (including long-lived RunStream handlers) will lack endpoint, pluginId, dsName/dsUID and uname, making the extracted ContextualLoggerMiddleware incomplete and its behaviour inconsistent across endpoints.

No test covers contextual-logger propagation or the LoggerMiddleware field move

The refactor removes the explicit pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname fields from LoggerMiddleware.logRequest and relies entirely on ContextualLoggerMiddleware enriching the context earlier in the chain plus Logger.FromContext honouring it, yet the only renamed test still asserts Prometheus metrics and never checks the context seen downstream or the emitted Plugin Request Completed fields. A regression in middleware ordering or in FromContext (in either the real or fake logger) that drops those log fields would pass the whole suite undetected; a chain-level test for the new middleware is needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes on a nil host instead of failing validation

The before_validation block calls self.host.sub! unconditionally. When host is nil (EmbeddableHost.new with no attributes, or a create/update request missing the host param), this raises NoMethodError and produces a 500 rather than a validation error rendered by render_json_error. There is also no presence validation for host or category_id. Guard the normalization for blank values and add a presence validation so invalid input is reported cleanly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the before_validation callback unconditionally calls self.host.sub!, raising NoMethodError when host is nil. The candidate's additional validation suggestions do not change this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Update and destroy raise NoMethodError for a nonexistent host id

Both update (line 10) and destroy (line 15) use EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first and then immediately call save_host(host) or host.destroy. For a stale or invalid id the record is nil, so save_host fails setting host.host and destroy fails on nil.destroy, returning a 500 instead of a 404. Look the record up with find (letting ActiveRecord raise RecordNotFound) or explicitly render a not-found error when it is absent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing existence check in update and destroy: the ID lookup can return nil, and subsequent save_host or destroy calls cause a NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration inserts legacy hosts verbatim, bypassing normalization, so migrated hosts stop matching

Legacy embeddable_hosts values are inserted with raw SQL instead of going through EmbeddableHost, so the model's before_validation stripping of scheme and path never runs. Values previously accepted and handled by SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host? such as 'http://discourse.org' or 'https://example.com/1234' are stored verbatim, while EmbeddableHost.record_for_host compares lower(host) against URI(referer).host (e.g. 'discourse.org'), so those migrated hosts will never be allowed after the upgrade and embedding silently breaks for them. The unescaped interpolation of h into the INSERT also breaks the migration if a stored value contains a single quote. Normalize (and safely quote/bind) each host before inserting it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: raw SQL migration bypasses EmbeddableHost normalization, leaving schemes and paths in legacy values that fail bare-host lookups. Its additional SQL quoting concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Category and embeddable-host fabricator file contents are swapped

spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb now contains only the embeddable_host fabricator, while the newly added spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb contains all of the category fabricators (category, diff_category, happy_category, private_category). Tests still pass because Fabrication loads every file regardless of name, but the mislabeled files are misleading and invite duplicate-definition mistakes when someone edits the file matching the fabricator name. Move each definition into the file named after it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: the category and embeddable-host fabricator file contents were swapped. The candidate differs in its assessment of the consequences, but clearly identifies the same file-content mix-up.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the legacy embed_category setting was never persisted

The migration dereferences execute(...)[0]['id'] for a query joining site_settings to categories on the embed_category setting. Site settings that were never customized are not stored as rows, so for the common case where embed_category was never set this query returns zero rows, [0] is nil, and nil['id'] raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and the deploy/upgrade. The fallback on lines 14-16 makes the same assumption about an uncategorized_category_id row existing. The migration must handle missing rows (e.g. check cmd_tuples / nil before indexing) and fall back safely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unchecked execute(...)[0]['id'] access, which crashes when the embed_category query returns no rows. The candidate adds details about migration failure and fallback handling without changing the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Host format validation is inconsistent with host lookup and rejects valid hosts

The format regex allows an optional port (:[0-9]{1,5}), but record_for_host looks up URI(host).host, which strips the port, so a saved host like 'example.com:8080' can never equal the stored string and will never be allowed or assigned a category. Conversely the regex restricts the TLD to 2-5 letters, rejecting valid embed hosts the old free-form setting accepted, such as example.museum or example.technology. Validation, storage normalization, and lookup need to agree on ports and TLD length.

No uniqueness constraint on host makes the host-to-category mapping ambiguous

Nothing prevents duplicate host rows: the model has no uniqueness validation and the migration creates the table without a unique index. An admin can create the same host twice with different categories, after which record_for_host's unordered .first picks an arbitrary row, so topics imported from that host are filed into a nondeterministic category and host_allowed?/category behavior depends on database row order. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness validation and a unique database index (after normalizing case in storage).

Clicking edit crashes when the host has no resolved category

The edit action does this.get('host.category.id') without checking that category exists. A host's category is undefined when its category was deleted, and also right after saving a new host without choosing a category: save() sets category from Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')) with a null categoryId while the server silently defaults to the uncategorized category, leaving host.category undefined in the client. Clicking the pencil then throws a TypeError and the row can no longer be edited until a page reload. Any other valid? check, or a save that ultimately fails for an unrelated reason such as the password, also records a match even though no account attempt completed. This spec expects TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve to be called, but EmbedController#best now calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, user_id: ..., embed_url: ...). The mocha expectation will therefore fail, and depending on test job settings the enqueued job may also run for real. The spec should expect Jobs.enqueue with :retrieve_topic and the correct arguments instead.

Import first queries TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url) and only creates the embed record if none exists, but concurrent PollFeed and RetrieveTopic jobs (the latter bypasses throttling for staff) can both observe no record for the same new URL and both create a topic/post. The unique database index on embed_url then makes one TopicEmbed.create! raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job and rolling back its work. The creation path needs to handle the uniqueness conflict or serialize creation per URL.

retrieved_recently? sets the Redis throttle key with setnx and only afterwards calls expire as a separate command. If the process crashes or Redis errors between the two commands, the key persists forever with no TTL, permanently blocking retrieval for that embed URL and leaving visitors on the loading page. The key should be created atomically with its 60-second expiry.

The import previously created the topic locally from the Disqus export, but now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...), which fetches t[:link] over HTTP. The removed --category option also means existing import invocations using it will fail and imported topics can no longer be placed in a category.

Any client that spoofs the Referer header (the only embeddable-host check is that header, trivially set by non-browser clients) can call embed/best with arbitrary distinct URLs on the embeddable host, and every miss enqueues a RetrieveTopic job. The only throttling is per exact URL string inside the job and TopicEmbed is keyed by the exact URL string, so adding random query parameters, fragments, or other variants of the same article bypasses the throttle, floods the job queue with server-side fetches of the remote host, and can create duplicate topics for the same article. Passing that comma-containing value as a StatsD/DogStatsD tag makes the backend parse it as `shard:0` plus stray tags `1` and `2`, so the produce, wait-produce, and segment-size metrics cannot be correctly attributed by shard. Emit these metrics per flushed segment/shard or otherwise use a single sanitized shard tag value.

test_flusher_processes_limit creates four shards mapped to two flusher processes, but it only asserts process counts and then joins without submitting spans or advancing the flush clock. The existing basic test covers only one shard/process, so the central new behavior—a shared process correctly flushing, producing, and completing segments for multiple shards, without drops or duplicates—is untested. Add an end-to-end test that stores spans across several shards with fewer flusher processes than shards and asserts the produced segments for each shard.

Rebalanced strategy reuses an irreversibly shut-down queue pool

The factory creates FixedQueuePool once during construction, while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() shuts that pool down. A normal Kafka rebalance can therefore cause silent data loss until the process is restarted.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

The commit loop can consequently commit the offset for a result that was never successfully handled, contradicting the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing and causing failed uptime results to be lost rather than redelivered.

Each work queue is created with queue.Queue() and therefore has no maximum size, and submit() never raises MessageRejected or otherwise blocks. If workers process more slowly than Kafka delivers, Arroyo can continue submitting messages indefinitely, growing memory use and hiding the backlog from Kafka flow control. This also makes the class documentation's claim of natural backpressure when queues fill up incorrect because these queues never fill.

Close stops offset committing before workers finish and shutdown drops queued work

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() stops and joins the commit thread before shutting down the queue pool, so results completed by workers afterward have no commit loop left to commit their offsets and will be redelivered. In addition, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False); a busy worker exits after its current item instead of draining its queue. Graceful close therefore both leaves processed offsets uncommitted and abandons queued work rather than finishing it within the strategy's join period.

get_queue_for_group() uses the built-in hash() for a string group key. Python randomizes string hashing per interpreter unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed, so the same subscription can map to different queues after a restart or when processed by another consumer process. That undermines the documented consistent-assignment and per-group ordering guarantee across rebalances and deployments; a stable digest such as hashlib.md5 or sha256 should be used instead.

The CLI accepts any integer for --max-workers, and this code converts 0 to 20 with 'or' while passing a negative value through as num_queues. A negative value creates no queues or workers; submissions then fail with an index/modulo error, are caught by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), and are marked complete, so their offsets can be committed without processing. The option should be validated as a positive integer before constructing the pool.

OffsetTracker retains every offset after a blocked or very slow offset, because offsets can only be removed after a contiguous commit. get_committable_offsets() is called once per second and computes both min() and max() over that retained set each time. During exactly the slow-item backlog this feature is meant to tolerate, the set can grow to a large number of completed offsets and the commit loop becomes repeated O(n) work while also retaining unbounded tracking state.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts span end-timestamp scores on overlaps

The old SUNIONSTORE deduplicated identical payloads without changing metadata. The new redis.call('zunionstore', set_key, 2, set_key, span_key) uses Redis' default AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both sorted sets (duplicate delivery, a merge of overlapping partial segments, or destination/source overlap) gets score roughly end_timestamp+end_timestamp instead of its end timestamp. That corrupts the score later used by zpopmin eviction, artificially protecting duplicated spans and causing other spans to be evicted first. Use an explicit AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN) to preserve one real timestamp.

SET-to-ZSET switch breaks in-flight Redis segments with WRONGTYPE errors

Existing buffered segment keys were created as Redis SETs by sadd and can remain live until the one-hour redis_ttl/flush timeouts expire. This change immediately issues ZADD in process_spans, and the Lua script likewise issues ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN, while flush uses ZSCAN. Redis returns WRONGTYPE when a sorted-set command is used on an existing SET key, so during rollout process_spans fails for traces already buffered, batches retry/stall, and unflushed spans can be lost when the old keys expire. The PR contains no key versioning, drain, dual-type handling, or other migration for in-flight keys.

Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed while insert cap ignores the configured limit

_load_segment_data no longer enforces SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans; after this change that constructor setting is effectively dead. Eviction is instead hardcoded to 1000 in add-buffer.lua, so the default changes from 1001 to 1000 and any custom max_segment_spans value is silently ignored. Segments that bypass insert eviction, including pre-existing large segments, are now loaded and emitted regardless of span count, bounded only by max_segment_bytes, increasing memory and downstream segment-size risk.

Redirect resolution depth silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The redirect-following loop previously allowed 10000 hops, with a comment acknowledging that deeper segment trees might not be joined correctly. Reducing it to 1000 makes that failure mode ten times more likely: when the cap is exhausted the script proceeds with an unresolved set_span_id and no error, so spans for a deep chain can be placed in a different segment key and flushed as split/incomplete segments rather than being joined to their root segment.

Insert-time eviction silently drops spans with no metric or truncation signal

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin permanently discards the earliest-ending spans during insert. Unlike the removed flush-time span-count guard, which emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded and logged the segment size, this path emits no metric/log and marks the flushed segment in no way as truncated. Operators cannot measure span loss and downstream consumers receive an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one.

No test covers the new eviction, sorted-set merge, or score behavior

The test changes only add the newly required end_timestamp_precise field to existing Span constructions. No test inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment, asserts which spans zpopmin retains, covers duplicate payloads across merged partial segments, or verifies that scores remain real end timestamps after ZUNIONSTORE. The central data-loss behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer dataset instead of the dataset actually being queried

_get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which is the dataset that will execute the query, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable dataset from the request. The dashboard-split factory calls _get_event_stats with different datasets, including discover for error splits and the scoped dataset for transaction-like splits. Consequently, an error split can incorrectly miss upsampling, while a metrics or transaction-like query can receive upsampled_count() even though that builder or table does not support sample_weight. The decision should be based on scoped_dataset and the query actually being executed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset. Both also tie it to the dashboard split path, where the query runs against discover and upsampling can be missed.

false_positives.candidate:
Error-focus detection ignores the actual query and uses a naive substring check

The transform decision reads only request.GET['query'] and checks whether it contains 'event.type:error'. _get_event_stats is not given the opportunity to pass its query argument, which may be an internally constructed dashboard query such as '(...) AND !event.type:transaction' or a widget query that differs from the request parameter. The substring check also misses forms such as '!event.type:transaction' and 'event.type:[error, default]', while incorrectly matching the negated query '!event.type:error'. Error charts can therefore remain unupsampled, or non-error queries can have count() replaced by a sum of sample_weight.

upsampled_count has no fallback for missing sample weights and truncates fractional weights

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). Events in an allowlisted project that were ingested before error sampling was enabled, or that otherwise have a null or zero sample_weight, contribute nothing instead of counting as one event, so historical and unsampled errors disappear from upsampled series. Additionally, toInt64 truncates fractional sums produced by float sample weights, systematically undercounting estimated errors. Missing weights should default to 1 and the fractional estimate should be rounded or retained rather than truncated.

Internal upsampled_count function is exposed as a public Discover function

The new SnQLFunction does not set private=True, unlike neighboring internal-only aggregation helpers. It therefore expands the public Discover function surface and can be requested directly through query builders using DiscoverDatasetConfig, bypassing the stats endpoint's project-allowlist and dataset checks. On non-allowlisted projects or datasets backed by tables without meaningful error sample weights, this can return misleading counts or produce invalid Snuba queries. The function should remain internal to the gated transformation.

Cached allowlist eligibility can remain stale and the invalidation helper is never used

Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds, but invalidate_upsampling_cache has no caller in this change and there is no hook from option changes to that helper. After a project is removed from issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist, the endpoint can continue replacing count() with upsampled counts; after a project is added, it can continue returning raw counts until the entry expires. Either wire invalidation to allowlist changes or remove the unused invalidation API and explicitly accept only TTL-based expiry.

Stray subproject file is unrelated to the feature

This change adds a root-level 'sentry-repo' file containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a'. That resembles an accidentally recorded nested-repository gitlink without any corresponding submodule configuration and is unrelated to error upsampling. It can confuse checkout and submodule tooling and should be removed before merging.

Tests do not exercise the public eligibility entry point used by the endpoint

The unit tests import and test only the private helpers _are_all_projects_error_upsampled, _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform, and the column transform. They do not test is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, the only function called by organization_events_stats, including its caching behavior, dataset handling, or interaction with a scoped/split dataset. The Snuba tests also cover only events that already carry client_sample_rate=0.1, leaving unsampled events and the resulting sample_weight behavior unverified, so regressions in the actual production path can pass the added tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored

The test named "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}; despite the comment saying this allows access, checkPermission treats a false map value as no permission, and the fake permission store also returns no granting permission. The request therefore denies through the ordinary cached/DB path even if permDenialCache is never consulted, so the test does not prove the new short-circuit works. It should configure the underlying store or permission cache to allow dash1, or assert that the permission store is not called when the denial entry is present.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points to the same problem as the golden comment. The test comment says the cache allows access, but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission treats that scope as not allowed. The candidate adds that this means the test doesn't actually check the denial cache, but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous

userPermDenialCacheKey joins variable-length UID, action, name, and parent values with plain underscores and no escaping, length prefixes, or hashing. Distinct tuples can consequently produce the same key: for example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. Grafana resource and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny a different resource until the entry expires. Build the key from a structured, unambiguously encoded or hashed tuple.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same problem: userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by joining components with plain underscores. Components can contain underscores, so distinct tuples can produce the same key and cause incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key does not include the identity type

The denial key is built only from namespace, the raw subject UID, action, resource name, and parent folder, but permission resolution switches on identity type and returns different permission sets for the same UID. In particular, anonymous and render-service subjects both use UID "0", while anonymous receives Viewer-role permissions and the render service is granted read access to all dashboards and folders. A denial recorded for anonymous:0 can therefore short-circuit and incorrectly deny render:0 for the same dashboard for up to the denial TTL, and the same collision can occur between user and service-account spellings. The key must include the identity type, preferably together with the canonical resolved UID.

Denial entries shadow fresher permissions and undermine immediate access after a grant

Check consults permDenialCache before checking the ordinary permission cache, and neither getUserPermissions' permission-cache refresh nor List's refresh deletes existing denial entries. After a permission is granted, such as the creator permission inserted for a new dashboard or folder, a later check or list for another resource can refresh permCache with a scope map that now allows the denied resource, yet checks for that resource will still return the old denial until the denial TTL expires. A denial recorded by a check made just before the grant has the same effect. This partially defeats the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created resources immediately; cached allowances should be honoured before denials or denials should be invalidated when permissions are refreshed.

Every distinct cached denial now forces a database permission fetch

When cached permissions do not allow a check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the permission-store cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so this performs a fresh database permission query. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent tuple for 30 seconds. A user checking many distinct dashboards or folders they do not own therefore causes one permission query per resource instead of one query per user/action as before, multiplying database load in denial-heavy or enumeration-heavy workloads and increasing cache cardinality. The revalidation needs a freshness or negative-cache strategy that does not scale database queries with the number of distinct denied resources.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The safe_urlopen call (and the unguarded get_user_info call that follows) should be covered by the same failure path that handles a missing access_token.

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation compares an organization-aware model against the raw updated model

update() obtains the original model through getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA-backed getForLogin result, however, is based on the stored enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC fields and does not exclude IdPs merely because their organization is disabled. Therefore, for an IdP in a disabled organization that currently qualifies in the stored data, changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly to a disqualifying value makes both the wrapped original and the updated model fail getLoginPredicate(), so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() returns without invalidating any login cache. The stale cached ID remains and can reappear when the organization is re-enabled, even though the IdP is now hidden or link-only. Empty-string organizationId collides with the null organization cache key

getForLogin() uses "" as the IdentityProviderListQuery search key when organizationId is null, while a caller-supplied organizationId of "" is also non-null and is kept as "". The cache therefore conflates the two cases, so getForLogin(ORG_ONLY or ALL, "") can return the cached all-organizations result, or the reverse ordering can make a null-organization request reuse an empty/specific-organization result. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

Multiple goroutines can concurrently observe a nil entryPointAssetsCache under the read lock, then queue on the write lock at line 48. Because the locked section does not re-check the cache, every queued goroutine re-reads and parses assets-manifest.json, overwrites the cache, and blocks other callers while holding the exclusive lock. A cold-start burst therefore defeats the cache and serializes redundant file I/O. After acquiring the lock, return the cached value when cfg.Env is not Dev and the cache is now populated, while preserving the reload behavior in Dev mode.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags unconditionally call r.log.Error before and after every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including successful batches and the final empty batch where err is nil and affected is 0. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs without justification

This changes the interval for CleanUpService.Run from 10 minutes to 1 minute. That ticker drives every job in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp-user invites, short URLs, and query-history enforcement will now run 10x as often, increasing database and log load in every Grafana instance. The PR description only justifies splitting the annotation DELETE statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks and does not mention or justify this frequency change, so it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or separately justified and scoped to annotations.

false_positives.candidate:
Parameter-limit workaround only handles SQLite, regressing large batches on other databases

deleteByIDs binds one '?' placeholder per fetched ID for every database except the special-cased SQLite path at lines 608-613. The previous implementation used a subquery DELETE with no per-ID bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable and this PR's own test raises it to 32767; a larger configured batch (over 65535 parameters) will now fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL with bind-parameter limits even though the old statement would have succeeded, aborting cleanup partway. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of up to batch-size IDs (32767 in the added test, applied repeatedly to annotations and orphaned tags) is O(n^2) in time and allocations and can make large cleanups and the new test very slow. However, it describes the inverse case: a legacy goroutine recording recordStorageDuration, rather than a storage failure recording recordLegacyDuration. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label

Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts legacy-versus-storage latency and error measurements and, for Delete, creates a high-cardinality kind label containing user object names.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. That is the same issue the golden comment describes.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object

Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result

Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete

Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes

The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility

The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. false_positives.candidate:

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale), while ApplicationController#set_locale is the only caller of I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Code outside a web request, such as background jobs and mailers, and translations using an explicit locale: option can therefore invoke the new Fallbacks backend before the site-default and :en YAML files have been lazily loaded. Existing or plugin code using the documented fallbacks API can therefore be silently ignored or fail, and regional locales can receive the site language instead of their parent language. The custom ordering should be implemented by subclassing or extending I18n::Locale::Fallbacks rather than replacing it with a plain Hash.

A correct dark-theme conversion must keep 30% for the light branch and use scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 70%) for the dark branch, but this line uses 70% for $primary and 30% for $secondary. Light-theme embedded-post usernames therefore become far paler than before and the dark-theme colour is far darker than intended, reducing readability in both themes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same change: the light-theme lightness went from 30% to 70% on the embedded-post username color, which lowers readability. The candidate adds that the light and dark values look swapped, but the core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In mobile/user.scss line 497, the lightness value for dark themes should be inverted to 70% instead of being changed to 50%. This change may lead to unintended visual regressions in light themes.

Mobile group-member name colour changes the original 30% lightness to 50%

The original rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). This line converts it to dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%)) instead of preserving 30% for light and using 70% on $secondary for dark. The light-theme name colour is therefore changed unnecessarily and the dark-theme colour is darker than the intended equivalent, weakening contrast.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the lightness was changed from 30% to 50% when it should have stayed at 30% for light themes and been inverted to 70% for dark themes. Both also note the unintended visual change in light themes.

false_positives.candidate:
Mobile topic-map heading colour changes the original 20% lightness to 50%

The original mobile rule was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), and the equivalent desktop topic-map heading correctly converts to 20% on $primary with 80% on $secondary for dark. This line instead uses 50% for both branches. Mobile topic-map headings become much paler in the light theme and much darker than intended in the dark theme, losing heading contrast.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
